questions.q: How fast does light travel through a vacuum, in kilometres per second?
questions.note: Light races along at 299,792 km per second, fast enough to circle the globe about seven and a half times in a single second.

questions.q: How fast does sound travel through air at 20 degrees Celsius, in metres per second?
questions.note: Sound moves at 343 metres per second in room-temperature air, which is why thunder always lags behind the lightning.

questions.q: How fast does sound travel through seawater, in metres per second?
questions.note: Sound zips through seawater at roughly 1,500 metres per second, more than four times its speed in air.

questions.q: What is absolute zero, the coldest possible temperature, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Absolute zero sits at -273 degrees Celsius (precisely -273.15), the point where atoms have the least possible energy.

questions.q: How many chemical elements are on the modern periodic table?
questions.note: The periodic table holds 118 elements, ending with oganesson, which was officially named in 2016.

questions.q: What is the atomic number of gold?
questions.note: Gold is element 79, and its symbol Au comes from aurum, the Latin word for shining dawn.

questions.q: How many protons are in the nucleus of a carbon atom?
questions.note: Carbon carries 6 protons, and this single number is what makes carbon carbon rather than anything else.

questions.q: What is the atomic number of uranium?
questions.note: Uranium is element 92, the heaviest element found in significant quantities in nature.

questions.q: How many rows, or periods, does the modern periodic table have?
questions.note: The periodic table has 7 periods, and the seventh row was only completed in 2016 when four new elements were named.

questions.q: How many columns, or groups, does the modern periodic table have?
questions.note: There are 18 groups, and elements in the same column tend to behave like chemical siblings.

questions.q: How many elements did Dmitri Mendeleev include in his first periodic table of 1869?
questions.note: Mendeleev arranged just 63 known elements, yet left gaps that correctly predicted elements discovered decades later.

questions.q: How many chemical elements are liquid at room temperature?
questions.note: Only 2 elements are liquid at room temperature: shimmering mercury and deep-red bromine.

questions.q: How many prize categories did Alfred Nobel establish in his will?
questions.note: Nobel's will created 5 prizes - physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace - with economics added only in 1968.

questions.q: At what temperature does gold melt, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Gold melts at 1,064 degrees Celsius, a property goldsmiths have exploited for over 6,000 years.

questions.q: At what temperature does iron melt, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Iron melts at 1,538 degrees Celsius, which is why the Iron Age had to wait for furnaces far hotter than any campfire.

questions.q: At what temperature does tungsten, the metal with the highest melting point, melt in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Tungsten holds out until 3,422 degrees Celsius, which made it perfect for old-fashioned lightbulb filaments.

questions.q: At what temperature does the metal mercury freeze solid, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Mercury freezes at about -39 degrees Celsius, which is why mercury thermometers fail in polar winters.

questions.q: At what temperature does liquid nitrogen boil, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Liquid nitrogen boils at -196 degrees Celsius, cold enough to freeze a rose so it shatters like glass.

questions.q: At what temperature does liquid helium boil, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Helium boils at -269 degrees Celsius, just four degrees above absolute zero, making it the coldest liquid known.

questions.q: At what temperature does pure ethanol boil, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Ethanol boils at 78 degrees Celsius, well below water, which is exactly what makes distillation possible.

questions.q: At what temperature does the metal sodium melt, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Sodium melts at just 98 degrees Celsius, so a pan of boiling water is hot enough to turn this metal to liquid.

questions.q: At what temperature does the metal gallium melt, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Gallium melts at 29.8 degrees Celsius, so a solid lump will slowly turn to liquid in the palm of your hand.

questions.q: What is the density of gold, in grams per cubic centimetre?
questions.note: Gold packs 19.3 grams into every cubic centimetre, so a standard bar the size of a brick weighs over 12 kilograms.

questions.q: What is the density of osmium, the densest naturally occurring element, in grams per cubic centimetre?
questions.note: Osmium crams 22.6 grams into each cubic centimetre, roughly twice the density of lead.

questions.q: What is the density of lithium, the lightest metal, in grams per cubic centimetre?
questions.note: At just 0.53 grams per cubic centimetre, lithium is about half the density of water and will happily float on it.

questions.q: At what temperature is liquid water at its most dense, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Water is densest at 4 degrees Celsius, which is why ponds freeze from the top down and fish survive underneath.

questions.q: By roughly what percentage does water expand when it freezes into ice?
questions.note: Water swells by about 9 percent as it freezes, which is why ice floats and forgotten bottles burst in the freezer.

questions.q: Roughly what percentage of an iceberg's volume sits above the waterline?
questions.note: Only about 10 percent of an iceberg shows above the water, which is where the phrase tip of the iceberg comes from.

questions.q: What percentage of average seawater is dissolved salt, by weight?
questions.note: Seawater is about 3.5 percent salt, meaning every litre carries roughly 35 grams of it.

questions.q: What percentage of Earth's atmosphere is oxygen?
questions.note: Oxygen makes up about 21 percent of the air, a balance that has kept animals breathing for hundreds of millions of years.

questions.q: What percentage of Earth's atmosphere is nitrogen?
questions.note: Nitrogen dominates the air at 78 percent, quietly diluting the oxygen we actually use.

questions.q: What percentage of Earth's crust is oxygen, by weight?
questions.note: Oxygen makes up a surprising 46.6 percent of the crust by weight, locked into rocks, sand and minerals.

questions.q: What percentage of Earth's crust is aluminium, the most abundant metal, by weight?
questions.note: Aluminium accounts for 8.1 percent of the crust, yet it was so hard to extract that it once cost more than gold.

questions.q: What is the pH of pure water?
questions.note: Pure water sits at pH 7, the exact neutral point between acid and alkaline.

questions.q: What is the approximate pH of lemon juice?
questions.note: Lemon juice registers around pH 2, roughly a hundred thousand times more acidic than pure water.

questions.q: What is the acceleration due to gravity at Earth's surface, in metres per second squared?
questions.note: Objects accelerate at 9.8 metres per second squared, so a dropped apple is falling at motorway speed within three seconds.

questions.q: What is standard atmospheric pressure at sea level, in hectopascals?
questions.note: Standard sea-level pressure is 1,013 hectopascals, the invisible weight of the entire atmosphere pressing down on you.

questions.q: To roughly what temperature can a lightning bolt heat the air around it, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: A lightning channel can reach around 30,000 degrees Celsius, about five times hotter than the surface of the sun.

questions.q: How many seconds does thunder take to travel one kilometre from a lightning strike?
questions.note: Thunder takes about 3 seconds per kilometre, so counting the gap after a flash tells you how far away the storm is.

questions.q: What is the approximate wavelength of red light, the longest the human eye can see, in nanometres?
questions.note: Red light waves measure about 700 nanometres, roughly a hundredth the width of a human hair.

questions.q: What is the frequency of the standard tuning note A above middle C, in hertz?
questions.note: Orchestras worldwide tune to A at 440 hertz, a standard formally adopted by ISO in 1955.

questions.q: How loud is a jet aircraft at take-off from close range, in decibels?
questions.note: A jet at take-off roars at about 140 decibels, loud enough to cause pain and instant hearing damage without protection.

questions.q: At what frequency do domestic microwave ovens operate, in megahertz?
questions.note: Microwave ovens hum along at 2,450 megahertz, almost the same frequency your Wi-Fi router uses.

questions.q: What is the standard mains electricity voltage in Europe, in volts?
questions.note: European sockets deliver 230 volts, roughly double the 120 volts used across North America.

questions.q: What is the voltage of a standard AA alkaline battery, in volts?
questions.note: An AA battery supplies 1.5 volts, a standard so useful it has barely changed in over a century.

questions.q: To roughly what temperature does water boil inside a sealed pressure cooker, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Under pressure, water boils at about 120 degrees Celsius instead of 100, which is why pressure cookers work so fast.

questions.q: How many million volts can a single bolt of lightning carry?
questions.note: A lightning bolt can pack about 300 million volts, thousands of times more than the most powerful transmission lines.

questions.q: How many karats is pure gold?
questions.note: Pure gold is 24 karats, so an 18-karat ring is eighteen twenty-fourths gold and the rest sturdier metals.

questions.q: What percentage of 18-karat gold is actually gold?
questions.note: 18-karat gold is 75 percent pure gold, with copper and silver added for strength and colour.

questions.q: What percentage of sterling silver is pure silver?
questions.note: Sterling silver is 92.5 percent silver, a standard so old it appears in English records from the 13th century.

questions.q: What is the hardness of quartz on the Mohs scale?
questions.note: Quartz scores 7 on the Mohs scale, hard enough to scratch glass and steel alike.

questions.q: How many colours did Isaac Newton name in the rainbow?
questions.note: Newton named 7 colours, adding indigo partly because he wanted the spectrum to match the seven notes of a musical scale.

questions.q: How many sides does a classic snowflake crystal have?
questions.note: Snowflakes grow with 6 sides because water molecules lock together in hexagons as they freeze.

questions.q: How many atoms make up a single molecule of water?
questions.note: A water molecule has just 3 atoms - two hydrogens and one oxygen - hence the famous formula H2O.

questions.q: How many laws of motion did Isaac Newton set out in his Principia?
questions.note: Newton needed only 3 laws of motion to explain everything from falling apples to orbiting moons.

questions.q: How many types, or flavours, of quark exist in the standard model of particle physics?
questions.note: There are 6 quark flavours, with the whimsical names up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom.

questions.q: How long is the circular tunnel of the Large Hadron Collider, in kilometres?
questions.note: The LHC's ring runs 27 kilometres beneath the French-Swiss border, making it the largest machine ever built.

questions.q: What is the half-life of carbon-14, used to date ancient objects, in years?
questions.note: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years, which lets archaeologists date anything organic back about 50,000 years.

questions.q: What is the half-life of uranium-238, in billions of years?
questions.note: Uranium-238's half-life of 4.5 billion years matches the age of the Earth, so half the planet's original supply is still here.

questions.q: How fast does light travel through glass, in kilometres per second?
questions.note: Light slows to about 200,000 km per second in glass, roughly two-thirds of its vacuum speed, which is what makes lenses bend it.

questions.q: How many times could light circle the Earth in one second?
questions.note: Light could lap the equator about 7.5 times every second, which is why you see a distant lightning flash essentially instantly while its thunder takes seconds to arrive.

questions.q: At roughly what temperature does water boil at the summit of Mount Everest, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: With so little air pressure, water on Everest's summit boils at about 71 degrees Celsius - too cool to brew a decent cup of tea.

questions.q: At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales read exactly the same number?
questions.note: At -40 degrees the two scales meet exactly, a coincidence beloved of physics teachers everywhere.

questions.q: At what temperature does water boil at sea level on the Fahrenheit scale?
questions.note: Water boils at 212 degrees Fahrenheit, exactly 180 Fahrenheit degrees above its freezing point of 32.

questions.q: How fast can a tsunami travel across the deep open ocean, in kilometres per hour?
questions.note: In deep water a tsunami can race at 800 km/h, as fast as a jet airliner, yet pass under ships almost unnoticed.

questions.q: What wind speed was recorded at Mount Washington in 1934, long the fastest ever measured at Earth's surface, in kilometres per hour?
questions.note: The 1934 gust hit 372 km/h, and the weather crew's log entry simply celebrated that their instruments had survived.

questions.q: What was the diameter of the largest hailstone ever recorded in the United States, which fell in South Dakota in 2010, in centimetres?
questions.note: The Vivian hailstone measured 20 centimetres across - about the size of a volleyball - and weighed nearly a kilogram.

questions.q: How deep is the Kola Superdeep Borehole, the deepest hole ever drilled into the Earth, in kilometres?
questions.note: Soviet engineers drilled 12.3 kilometres down, yet reached barely a third of the way through the continental crust.

questions.q: What percentage of the energy needed to make new aluminium is saved by recycling it instead?
questions.note: Recycling aluminium saves about 95 percent of the energy, so a can can be back on the shelf within 60 days.

questions.q: At roughly what temperature does sand melt to form glass, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Pure silica sand melts at about 1,700 degrees Celsius, which is why glassmakers add soda ash to lower the heat required.

questions.q: In which year did Albert Einstein publish his theory of special relativity?
questions.note: Einstein published special relativity in 1905, his miracle year, while working as a patent clerk in Bern.

questions.q: In which year did Isaac Newton publish his Principia Mathematica?
questions.note: The Principia appeared in 1687, funded personally by Edmond Halley of comet fame after the Royal Society ran short of money.

questions.q: In which year did Marie Curie win her first Nobel Prize?
questions.note: Marie Curie shared the 1903 physics prize, becoming the first woman laureate, and later won again in chemistry in 1911.

questions.q: In which year did Alexander Fleming discover penicillin?
questions.note: Fleming spotted the mould in 1928 on a petri dish he had left out while on holiday, and medicine was never the same.

questions.q: In which year did James Watson and Francis Crick describe the double-helix structure of DNA?
questions.note: The double helix was unveiled in 1953 in a Nature paper barely one page long, building on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images.

questions.q: In which year did Alexander Graham Bell patent the telephone?
questions.note: Bell's telephone patent was granted in 1876, mere hours ahead of a rival filing by Elisha Gray.

questions.q: In which year did Thomas Edison demonstrate his first commercially practical incandescent light bulb?
questions.note: Edison's bulb glowed in 1879 after his team tested thousands of possible filament materials, including bamboo.

questions.q: Around which year did Johannes Gutenberg develop his movable-type printing press in Europe?
questions.note: Gutenberg developed his press around 1440, and within 50 years printing shops had spread across Europe.

questions.q: In which year did Tim Berners-Lee propose the World Wide Web?
questions.note: Berners-Lee submitted his proposal at CERN in 1989, and his boss famously scribbled on it: vague, but exciting.

questions.q: In which year did Wilhelm Röntgen discover X-rays?
questions.note: Röntgen found X-rays in 1895 and won the very first Nobel Prize in Physics for it; he refused to patent the discovery.

questions.q: In which year did Edward Jenner carry out his first smallpox vaccination?
questions.note: Jenner performed his first vaccination in 1796, and the word vaccine itself comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

questions.q: In which year did Alfred Nobel patent dynamite?
questions.note: Nobel patented dynamite in 1867, and the fortune it earned him later funded the prizes that bear his name.

questions.q: In which year were the first Nobel Prizes awarded?
questions.note: The first Nobel Prizes were handed out in 1901, five years after Alfred Nobel's death.

questions.q: In which year was the transistor invented at Bell Labs?
questions.note: The transistor was born in 1947, and billions of its descendants now sit inside every phone in every pocket.

questions.q: In which year was the first working laser demonstrated?
questions.note: Theodore Maiman fired up the first laser in 1960 using a ruby crystal, and it was famously called a solution looking for a problem.

questions.q: In which year did Dmitri Mendeleev publish his periodic table of the elements?
questions.note: Mendeleev published his table in 1869, reportedly after the arrangement came to him in a dream.

questions.q: In which year did Anders Celsius propose his temperature scale?
questions.note: Celsius proposed his scale in 1742, though he originally set 0 as boiling and 100 as freezing - it was flipped after his death.

questions.q: Around which year did Nicéphore Niépce capture the world's first surviving photograph?
questions.note: Niépce made his rooftop image around 1826, with an exposure believed to have taken at least eight hours.

questions.q: In which year did John Logie Baird give the first public demonstration of television?
questions.note: Baird showed off working television in 1926 to scientists in a London attic, using a contraption partly built from a hatbox.

questions.q: In which year was ENIAC, one of the first general-purpose electronic computers, unveiled?
questions.note: ENIAC was unveiled in 1946, weighed about 27 tonnes and filled a room, yet had less power than a pocket calculator.

questions.q: In which year was the first call made from a handheld mobile phone?
questions.note: Motorola's Martin Cooper made the first handheld mobile call in 1973 - to his rival at Bell Labs, just to gloat.

questions.q: In which year did Alessandro Volta invent the first electric battery?
questions.note: Volta stacked his pile of zinc and copper discs in 1800, and the volt is named in his honour.

questions.q: In which year did James Watt patent his improved steam engine?
questions.note: Watt patented his separate-condenser engine in 1769, a tweak that helped power the entire Industrial Revolution.

questions.q: In which year did Wallace Carothers and his DuPont team first create nylon?
questions.note: Nylon was created in 1935, and when nylon stockings launched in 1940 they sold out at a rate of thousands per hour.

questions.q: In which year did Bayer chemist Felix Hoffmann first synthesise aspirin in a stable form?
questions.note: Hoffmann synthesised aspirin in 1897, turning a remedy hinted at by willow bark into one of the world's most used medicines.

questions.q: In which year did CERN announce the discovery of the Higgs boson?
questions.note: CERN announced the Higgs boson in 2012, confirming a particle first predicted back in 1964.

questions.q: In which year did Percy Spencer file his patent for the microwave oven?
questions.note: Spencer filed his patent in 1945 after a radar magnetron melted the chocolate bar in his pocket.

questions.q: By roughly how many centimetres can the Eiffel Tower grow taller on a hot summer day?
questions.source: Société d'Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel
questions.note: Thermal expansion can add about 15 cm — the iron shrinks back every night.

questions.q: What is the approximate wavelength of blue light, in nanometres?
questions.note: About 450 nm — shorter than red light's 700 nm, which is why blue scatters more in the sky.

questions.q: How many seconds are there in a 24-hour day?
questions.note: 86,400 — and thanks to the Moon's pull, days are lengthening by about 2 milliseconds per century.

questions.q: In which year did Apollo 11 first land humans on the Moon?
questions.note: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin touched down on 20 July 1969, watched live by around 600 million people.

questions.q: In which year did the Soviet Union launch Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite?
questions.note: Sputnik 1 went up on 4 October 1957, beeping its way around the Earth and kicking off the Space Age.

questions.q: In which year did Yuri Gagarin become the first human in space?
questions.note: Gagarin orbited the Earth once aboard Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961.

questions.q: In which year were the twin Voyager probes launched?
questions.note: Both Voyagers left Earth in 1977 and are still sending data from beyond the planets nearly half a century later.

questions.q: In which year was the Hubble Space Telescope launched?
questions.note: Hubble rode Space Shuttle Discovery to orbit in 1990 and needed corrective optics fitted three years later.

questions.q: In which year was the planet Neptune discovered?
questions.note: Neptune was found in 1846 almost exactly where mathematicians predicted it would be, using pen-and-paper calculations.

questions.q: In which year did Clyde Tombaugh discover Pluto?
questions.note: Tombaugh spotted Pluto in 1930 by comparing photographic plates at Lowell Observatory in Arizona.

questions.q: In which year did the International Astronomical Union reclassify Pluto as a dwarf planet?
questions.note: The 2006 vote in Prague demoted Pluto after 76 years as the ninth planet.

questions.q: In which year did the Apollo 13 crew survive their famous 'successful failure' mission?
questions.note: An oxygen tank ruptured on the way to the Moon in April 1970, yet all three astronauts made it home safely.

questions.q: In which year did Apollo 17, the last crewed Moon landing, take place?
questions.note: Gene Cernan left the final bootprints in December 1972, and no one has walked there since.

questions.q: In which year did Halley's Comet last pass close to the Sun?
questions.note: Halley's 1986 visit was met by a small fleet of spacecraft, including Europe's Giotto probe.

questions.q: In which year is Halley's Comet next predicted to return to the inner solar system?
questions.note: Halley swings by roughly every 76 years, so its next appearance is due in 2061.

questions.q: In which year did Voyager 1 become the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space?
questions.note: Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause in 2012, 35 years after leaving Earth.

questions.q: In which year did the Cassini spacecraft end its mission by plunging into Saturn?
questions.note: Cassini's 2017 Grand Finale dive protected Saturn's moons from any chance of contamination.

questions.q: In which year did NASA's New Horizons spacecraft fly past Pluto?
questions.note: New Horizons zipped past Pluto in 2015 after a nine-and-a-half-year journey, revealing a heart-shaped plain.

questions.q: In which year did the Space Shuttle make its first orbital flight?
questions.note: Columbia flew the first shuttle mission in April 1981 with just two astronauts aboard.

questions.q: In which year did Sally Ride become the first American woman in space?
questions.note: Sally Ride flew aboard Space Shuttle Challenger in 1983 at the age of 32.

questions.q: In which year did Alexei Leonov perform the first spacewalk?
questions.note: Leonov floated outside his Voskhod capsule for about 12 minutes in March 1965.

questions.q: In which year did Galileo first observe the four largest moons of Jupiter?
questions.note: Galileo spotted Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto in 1610 with a homemade telescope.

questions.q: In which year was the first planet found orbiting a Sun-like star beyond our solar system?
questions.source: Nobel Prize (Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences)
questions.note: 51 Pegasi b was announced in 1995 and later earned its discoverers a Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.q: In which year did the Philae lander touch down on a comet, a historic first?
questions.note: ESA's Philae bounced to a stop on comet 67P in 2014 after a ten-year chase aboard Rosetta.

questions.q: In which year was the James Webb Space Telescope launched?
questions.note: Webb lifted off on Christmas Day 2021 and unfolded itself perfectly on the way to its distant post.

questions.q: In which year did astronauts begin living aboard the International Space Station without interruption?
questions.note: The first resident crew arrived in November 2000, and the station has been continuously occupied ever since.

questions.q: In which year did the United States launch Skylab, its first space station?
questions.note: Skylab went up in 1973 and hosted three crews before falling back to Earth in 1979.

questions.q: In which year did a solar eclipse expedition famously confirm Einstein's theory of general relativity?
questions.note: Arthur Eddington's 1919 eclipse measurements showed starlight bending around the Sun, making Einstein world-famous.

questions.q: In which year was NASA founded?
questions.note: NASA opened for business in October 1958, a year after Sputnik spurred the United States into action.

questions.q: In which year was the first-ever image of a black hole revealed?
questions.note: The glowing ring of the black hole in galaxy M87 was unveiled in 2019, stitched together from telescopes across the globe.

questions.q: In which year did Apollo 8 carry the first humans around the Moon?
questions.note: Apollo 8 orbited the Moon at Christmas 1968 and brought home the famous Earthrise photograph.

questions.q: In which year did a spacecraft first photograph the far side of the Moon?
questions.note: The Soviet probe Luna 3 sent back the first grainy pictures of the Moon's hidden face in 1959.

questions.q: In which year did comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 crash into Jupiter?
questions.note: The comet's fragments slammed into Jupiter in 1994, leaving dark scars larger than the Earth.

questions.q: How far is the Moon from the Earth on average?
questions.note: The average distance is 384,400 km — you could line up about 30 Earths in the gap.

questions.q: How far is the Earth from the Sun on average, in millions of kilometres?
questions.note: The average is about 150 million km, a distance astronomers call one astronomical unit.

questions.q: How many moons does Mars have?
questions.note: Mars has 2 small moons, Phobos and Deimos, both likely captured asteroids.

questions.q: How many planets are there in our solar system?
questions.note: There are 8 planets since Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

questions.q: At roughly what altitude does the International Space Station orbit the Earth?
questions.note: The ISS circles about 400 km up — roughly the distance of London to Paris, straight overhead.

questions.q: How fast does the International Space Station travel as it orbits the Earth?
questions.note: At about 28,000 km/h the ISS laps the planet every 90 minutes, giving its crew 16 sunrises a day.

questions.q: What is the approximate temperature of the Sun's visible surface?
questions.note: The surface simmers at about 5,500 °C, positively cool next to the 15-million-degree core.

questions.q: How many minutes does sunlight take to reach the Earth?
questions.note: Light takes about 8.3 minutes to cross the gap, so we always see the Sun as it was eight minutes ago.

questions.q: How long is a day on Mars in Earth hours?
questions.note: A Martian day, or sol, lasts 24.6 hours — close enough to Earth's that rover teams live on Mars time.

questions.q: How many Earth days does Venus take to spin once on its axis?
questions.note: Venus takes 243 Earth days to rotate once — longer than its 225-day year — and it spins backwards.

questions.q: How many Earth days does Mars take to orbit the Sun?
questions.note: A Martian year lasts 687 Earth days, so birthdays there come round rather slowly.

questions.q: How many times more massive is Jupiter than the Earth?
questions.note: Jupiter weighs in at 318 Earth masses — more than twice all the other planets combined.

questions.q: How many crewed Apollo missions successfully landed on the Moon?
questions.note: 6 Apollo missions landed between 1969 and 1972; Apollo 13 famously had to turn back.

questions.q: How many people have walked on the Moon?
questions.note: Just 12 people have walked on the Moon, all of them Apollo astronauts between 1969 and 1972.

questions.q: How fast does light travel through space, in kilometres per second?
questions.note: Light races along at about 300,000 km/s — fast enough to circle the Earth seven times in a second.

questions.q: How many light-years away is Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun?
questions.note: Proxima Centauri sits 4.2 light-years away — a journey of tens of thousands of years with today's rockets.

questions.q: Roughly how many light-years across is the Milky Way galaxy?
questions.note: Our galaxy spans about 100,000 light-years and contains hundreds of billions of stars.

questions.q: How many Earths could you line up across the diameter of the Sun?
questions.note: About 109 Earths would fit across the Sun's face, and over a million inside it.

questions.q: What is the diameter of the Moon?
questions.note: At 3,475 km across, the Moon is about as wide as Australia.

questions.q: How tall is Olympus Mons on Mars, the largest volcano in the solar system?
questions.note: Olympus Mons rises about 22 km — nearly two and a half times the height of Mount Everest.

questions.q: What percentage of Earth's surface gravity would you feel standing on the Moon?
questions.note: Lunar gravity is about 17% of Earth's, which is why Apollo astronauts bounded like kangaroos.

questions.q: Greetings in how many languages are carried on the Voyager Golden Record?
questions.note: The record carries greetings in 55 languages, plus whale song and Chuck Berry, for any aliens who find it.

questions.q: What is the average surface temperature on Venus, the hottest planet?
questions.note: Venus bakes at about 465 °C under its thick carbon dioxide blanket — hot enough to melt lead.

questions.q: How fast can the strongest winds blow on Neptune?
questions.note: Neptune's winds can reach about 2,100 km/h, the fastest in the solar system.

questions.q: By how many degrees is Uranus tilted on its axis?
questions.note: Uranus is tipped over by about 98 degrees, so it essentially rolls around the Sun on its side.

questions.q: What is the average density of Saturn in grams per cubic centimetre?
questions.note: At just 0.69 g/cm³ Saturn is less dense than water — it would float in a big enough bathtub.

questions.q: How fast is the Earth's surface moving at the equator due to the planet's rotation?
questions.note: The equator whips along at about 1,670 km/h, yet we feel nothing because the motion is so smooth.

questions.q: How many centimetres farther from Earth does the Moon drift each year?
questions.note: The Moon retreats about 3.8 cm a year, measured by bouncing lasers off Apollo-era mirrors.

questions.q: How tall was the Saturn V rocket that launched astronauts to the Moon?
questions.note: The Saturn V stood 111 metres tall, higher than the Statue of Liberty including its pedestal.

questions.q: What is the diameter of the Hubble Space Telescope's main mirror?
questions.note: Hubble's 2.4-metre mirror was famously ground to the wrong shape and fixed by astronauts in 1993.

questions.q: What is the diameter of the James Webb Space Telescope's main mirror?
questions.note: Webb's 6.5-metre golden mirror is made of 18 hexagonal segments that unfolded in space.

questions.q: How many missions did NASA's Space Shuttle fleet fly in total?
questions.note: The shuttles flew 135 missions between 1981 and 2011.

questions.q: How many days did Valeri Polyakov spend in space on the longest single spaceflight?
questions.note: Polyakov spent 437 days aboard the Mir space station in 1994-95, a record that still stands.

questions.q: How many kilograms of Moon rock did the Apollo missions bring back to Earth?
questions.note: Apollo astronauts hauled home 382 kg of lunar samples, still being studied today.

questions.q: How long is the International Space Station from end to end?
questions.note: At 109 metres, the ISS is about the length of a football pitch and easily visible to the naked eye.

questions.q: What is the diameter of Pluto?
questions.note: New Horizons measured Pluto at 2,377 km across — smaller than Earth's Moon.

questions.q: How many official constellations divide up the night sky?
questions.note: The IAU recognises exactly 88 constellations, a list fixed in 1922.

questions.q: How many millions of light-years away is the Andromeda Galaxy?
questions.note: Andromeda lies 2.5 million light-years away, yet it is still visible to the naked eye on dark nights.

questions.q: How old is the universe in billions of years?
questions.note: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, dated by the afterglow of the Big Bang.

questions.q: What percentage of the solar system's total mass is contained in the Sun?
questions.note: The Sun holds about 99.8% of the solar system's mass — everything else is leftovers.

questions.q: How many large moons of Jupiter did Galileo discover with his telescope?
questions.note: Galileo found 4 — Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto — still known as the Galilean moons.

questions.q: How many days did the entire Apollo 11 mission last, from launch to splashdown?
questions.note: The whole trip took just over 8 days — about the length of a package holiday, with a Moon landing included.

questions.q: How fast must a rocket travel to escape Earth's gravity, in kilometres per second?
questions.note: Escape velocity is 11.2 km/s — about 40,000 km/h, or London to New York in nine minutes.

questions.q: What is the temperature of deep space, measured from the cosmic microwave background, in kelvin?
questions.note: The universe's background glow measures just 2.7 kelvin — about minus 270 °C.

questions.q: How old was John Glenn when he returned to space in 1998 as the oldest person to fly there at the time?
questions.note: Glenn flew on Space Shuttle Discovery at 77, some 36 years after his first orbit of the Earth.

questions.q: How many days does the Moon take to cycle through all its phases, from full moon to full moon?
questions.note: The full cycle of phases takes 29.5 days, the origin of our word 'month'.

questions.q: At what altitude does the Kármán line, the commonly used boundary of space, sit?
questions.note: Space officially begins 100 km up — a line you could drive to in under an hour if roads went straight up.

questions.q: How many kilometres did the Mars rover Opportunity drive in total?
questions.note: Opportunity covered 45 km — the first off-world marathon — before a dust storm ended its mission.

questions.q: How many flights did the Ingenuity helicopter make on Mars before its final touchdown in 2024?
questions.note: Ingenuity flew 72 times, spectacularly beating its original plan of just five test hops.

questions.q: By how many degrees is the Earth tilted on its axis?
questions.note: Earth leans over by 23.4 degrees, and that tilt is the reason we have seasons.

questions.q: How fast did Apollo 10 travel returning from the Moon, the fastest any humans have ever gone?
questions.note: The Apollo 10 crew hit 39,897 km/h in May 1969, a human speed record that still stands.

questions.q: How far from Earth were the Apollo 13 crew at their most distant, the farthest humans have ever been?
questions.note: Swinging around the far side of the Moon, Apollo 13 reached 400,171 km from home in April 1970.

questions.q: How many times did Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space, orbit the Earth?
questions.note: Tereshkova completed 48 orbits over nearly three days in 1963 — more than all American astronauts combined at that point.

questions.q: How many minutes did Alan Shepard's 1961 flight, the first American spaceflight, last?
questions.note: Shepard's suborbital hop lasted about 15 minutes from launch to splashdown.

questions.q: How many Earth-sized planets orbit the star TRAPPIST-1, announced in 2017?
questions.note: TRAPPIST-1 hosts 7 rocky planets, several of them in the star's habitable zone.

questions.q: At what altitude do geostationary satellites orbit, hovering over one spot on Earth?
questions.note: At exactly 35,786 km up, a satellite's orbit matches Earth's spin, so it appears fixed in the sky.

questions.q: How many times more massive is the Sun than the Earth?
questions.note: The Sun outweighs the Earth by about 333,000 times.

questions.q: From how many billions of kilometres away did Voyager 1 take the famous 'Pale Blue Dot' photo of Earth?
questions.note: Voyager 1 looked back from 6 billion km in 1990, catching Earth as a single pale pixel.

questions.q: How wide was the famous Arecibo radio telescope dish in Puerto Rico?
questions.note: Arecibo's 305-metre dish was the world's largest single-dish telescope for over 50 years, until China's 500-metre FAST telescope surpassed it in 2016; the dish collapsed in 2020.

questions.q: How many Earth years does Pluto take to orbit the Sun once?
questions.note: A Pluto year lasts 248 Earth years, so it has not completed a single orbit since its discovery in 1930.

questions.q: How many known moons does Pluto have?
questions.note: Pluto has 5 moons, and the largest, Charon, is so big the pair waltz around a shared point in space.

questions.q: How many planets can be seen from Earth with the naked eye?
questions.note: 5 planets — Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn — are visible without a telescope, as ancient stargazers knew.

questions.q: What is the diameter of the Earth?
questions.note: Earth measures 12,742 km across on average, bulging slightly at the equator.

questions.q: How long is a day on Jupiter in Earth hours?
questions.note: Giant Jupiter spins in just under 10 hours, the shortest day of any planet.

questions.q: What percentage of Earth's surface gravity would you feel standing on Mars?
questions.note: Martian gravity is about 38% of Earth's, so a 100 kg astronaut would feel like 38 kg.

questions.q: How much did Sputnik 1, the first satellite, weigh?
questions.note: Sputnik 1 weighed 83.6 kg — about the same as an adult man — and was only 58 cm across.

questions.q: How far is Neptune from the Sun, in billions of kilometres?
questions.note: Neptune orbits about 4.5 billion km out — 30 times farther from the Sun than the Earth.

questions.q: How many millions of tonnes of hydrogen does the Sun fuse every second?
questions.note: The Sun burns through about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen each second, and will keep going for billions of years.

questions.q: How fast did the Parker Solar Probe travel during its record-breaking 2024 flyby of the Sun?
questions.note: Parker reached about 692,000 km/h in December 2024, the fastest any human-made object has ever moved.

questions.q: How wide is Meteor Crater in Arizona, the best-preserved impact crater on Earth?
questions.note: The crater spans 1.2 km, blasted out by a metal asteroid roughly 50,000 years ago.

questions.q: What top speed, in km/h, can a cheetah reach in a short sprint?
questions.note: A cheetah can hit around 112 km/h, but only for a few hundred metres before it must rest.

questions.q: How fast, in km/h, was the record-setting peregrine falcon Frightful clocked in a dive in 1999?
questions.note: Frightful reached 389 km/h, making the peregrine falcon the fastest animal on Earth in a dive.

questions.q: How fast, in km/h, can an ostrich run at full sprint?
questions.note: An ostrich can sprint at about 70 km/h, making it the fastest animal on two legs.

questions.q: How fast, in km/h, does a peacock mantis shrimp throw its club-like punch underwater?
questions.note: The punch accelerates to about 80 km/h, one of the fastest strikes in the animal kingdom.

questions.q: How much can a blue whale, the largest animal ever known, weigh in tonnes?
questions.note: At up to 180 tonnes, a blue whale outweighs even the biggest dinosaurs.

questions.q: How much does a large male African elephant weigh, in tonnes?
questions.note: A big bull African elephant weighs about 6 tonnes, roughly the same as four family cars.

questions.q: How much does an ostrich egg, the largest egg of any living bird, typically weigh in kilograms?
questions.note: At about 1.4 kg, one ostrich egg holds roughly the same as two dozen chicken eggs.

questions.q: How much does the bee hummingbird, the world's smallest bird, weigh in grams?
questions.note: Cuba's bee hummingbird weighs about 2 grams, lighter than a single playing card.

questions.q: How much does a newborn giant panda cub weigh, in grams?
questions.note: A newborn panda weighs only about 100 grams, roughly 1/900th of its mother's weight.

questions.q: How much does a sperm whale's brain, the largest of any animal, weigh in kilograms?
questions.note: At about 7.8 kg, the sperm whale's brain is more than five times heavier than a human's.

questions.q: How much did the colossal squid landed by fishermen in 2007, the largest ever recorded, weigh in kilograms?
questions.source: Te Papa, Museum of New Zealand
questions.note: The 2007 specimen weighed 495 kg and is now displayed at Te Papa museum in Wellington.

questions.q: How much did the largest leatherback turtle ever recorded, found in Wales in 1988, weigh in kilograms?
questions.note: The Harlech leatherback weighed 916 kg, about as much as a small car.

questions.q: How much can the goliath frog, the world's largest frog, weigh in kilograms?
questions.note: West Africa's goliath frog can reach 3.3 kg, about the weight of a newborn human baby.

questions.q: How much can a large male Siberian tiger weigh, in kilograms?
questions.note: A big Siberian male can reach about 300 kg, making it the largest of all the big cats.

questions.q: How much can a large male polar bear weigh, in kilograms?
questions.note: A big male polar bear can weigh around 600 kg, the largest land carnivore on Earth.

questions.q: How much did the record fleece shorn from Chris the sheep in Australia in 2015 weigh, in kilograms?
questions.note: Chris had wandered wild for years and yielded a record 41 kg fleece in a single shearing.

questions.q: How tall can a male giraffe, the tallest living animal, grow in metres?
questions.note: A male giraffe can stand about 5.5 metres tall, high enough to peer into a second-storey window.

questions.q: How long can a blue whale grow, in metres?
questions.note: At up to 30 metres, a blue whale is about as long as three buses parked end to end.

questions.q: How long can a whale shark, the largest fish in the sea, grow in metres?
questions.note: Whale sharks reach about 12 metres yet feed almost entirely on tiny plankton.

questions.q: How long can a great white shark grow, in metres?
questions.note: The biggest great whites reach about 6 metres, longer than most family cars.

questions.q: How long is Medusa, the reticulated python recognised in 2011 as the longest snake in captivity, in metres?
questions.note: Medusa measured 7.67 metres and needed about 15 people to hold her at full length.

questions.q: How long was Lolong, the largest saltwater crocodile ever measured in captivity, in metres?
questions.note: Lolong, caught in the Philippines, measured 6.17 metres from snout to tail.

questions.q: How long can a Komodo dragon, the world's largest lizard, grow in metres?
questions.note: Komodo dragons reach about 3 metres and live only on a handful of Indonesian islands.

questions.q: How long can a giant squid grow, including its two long feeding tentacles, in metres?
questions.note: Female giant squid can reach about 13 metres, yet a live one was not filmed in the deep until 2012.

questions.q: What is the diameter of a giant squid's eye, the largest in the animal kingdom, in centimetres?
questions.note: At about 27 cm across, a giant squid's eye is the size of a dinner plate.

questions.q: How long is a giraffe's tongue, in centimetres?
questions.note: A giraffe's blue-black tongue is about 50 cm long, perfect for stripping thorny acacia branches.

questions.q: How long can a narwhal's spiral tusk grow, in metres?
questions.note: The tusk, actually an enormous tooth, can grow about 3 metres long and inspired unicorn legends.

questions.q: How wide can a giant oceanic manta ray's wingspan reach, in metres?
questions.note: Giant mantas can span about 7 metres from wingtip to wingtip, the widest of any ray.

questions.q: How long can the Chinese giant salamander, the world's largest amphibian, grow in metres?
questions.note: At up to 1.8 metres, this salamander is longer than many adult humans are tall.

questions.q: How long was the record-breaking Chinese stick insect described in 2016, the longest insect known, in centimetres?
questions.note: The stick insect measured 62.4 cm with legs outstretched, longer than your forearm.

questions.q: What leg span can the goliath birdeater, the world's biggest spider, reach in centimetres?
questions.note: The goliath birdeater of South America can span 28 cm, about the size of a dinner plate.

questions.q: What is the largest wingspan ever measured on a wandering albatross, in metres?
questions.note: At 3.63 metres, the wandering albatross holds the record wingspan of any living bird.

questions.q: How tall was Sampson, the tallest horse ever recorded, born in England in 1846, in metres?
questions.note: Sampson the Shire horse stood 2.19 metres at the shoulder, taller than any horse since.

questions.q: How far can a red kangaroo travel in a single bound, in metres?
questions.note: A red kangaroo at speed can cover about 9 metres in one hop, roughly the length of a bus.

questions.q: How long is the world's largest beaver dam, in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park, in metres?
questions.note: At about 850 metres, the dam is so large it was first spotted in satellite images.

questions.q: How long is the vast Argentine ant supercolony discovered along Europe's Mediterranean coast, in kilometres?
questions.note: The supercolony stretches about 6,000 km from Italy to Spain, with ants that treat each other as nest-mates.

questions.q: Roughly how many years can a Greenland shark live, according to the 2016 dating study in Science?
questions.note: Eye-lens dating suggested lifespans of around 400 years, making it the longest-lived vertebrate.

questions.q: How old was Ming, the ocean quahog clam collected off Iceland in 2006, the oldest animal ever aged?
questions.note: Ming's shell rings showed it was 507 years old, born around the time of Columbus's voyages.

questions.q: Roughly how many hours does a typical adult mayfly live?
questions.note: Most adult mayflies live about 24 hours, just long enough to mate and lay eggs.

questions.q: How many years do periodical cicadas of the longest-cycle broods spend underground before emerging?
questions.note: After 17 years underground, whole broods emerge together in their millions.

questions.q: How many years did Bluey, the Australian cattle dog recognised as the oldest dog ever, live?
questions.note: Bluey worked cattle in Victoria for decades and lived to 29, a record that has stood since 1939.

questions.q: How many years did Creme Puff of Texas, the oldest cat on record, live?
questions.note: Creme Puff lived to 38, roughly double a typical cat's lifespan.

questions.q: How many years did Cookie, the Major Mitchell's cockatoo at Brookfield Zoo and oldest parrot on record, live?
questions.note: Cookie arrived at the zoo in 1934 and lived to 83, outlasting generations of keepers.

questions.q: How old was Jonathan the Seychelles giant tortoise, the oldest known living land animal, estimated to be in 2022?
questions.note: Jonathan was estimated at 190 in 2022 and has lived on the island of St Helena since 1882.

questions.q: How many months does an African elephant's pregnancy last, the longest of any land animal?
questions.note: At about 22 months, an elephant pregnancy lasts nearly two years.

questions.q: How many days does a red kangaroo's pregnancy last before the tiny joey crawls into the pouch?
questions.note: After just 33 days, a jellybean-sized joey climbs unaided into its mother's pouch.

questions.q: How many days does a Virginia opossum's pregnancy last, one of the shortest of any mammal?
questions.note: Opossum young are born after only about 13 days, each smaller than a honeybee.

questions.q: How many days does a horse's pregnancy typically last?
questions.note: A mare carries her foal for about 340 days, a little over 11 months.

questions.q: How many days does a chicken egg take to hatch?
questions.note: A chicken egg hatches after 21 days of incubation, a figure farmers have relied on for centuries.

questions.q: For roughly how many days does a male emperor penguin incubate the egg on his feet through the Antarctic winter?
questions.note: The male balances the egg on his feet for about 65 days in darkness and cold, eating nothing.

questions.q: A kiwi's egg is famously huge for the bird's size — about what percentage of the mother's body weight is it?
questions.note: A kiwi egg is about 20% of the mother's weight, proportionally the largest of any bird.

questions.q: How many eggs can an ocean sunfish carry at once, more than any other known vertebrate?
questions.note: A single sunfish can carry about 300 million eggs, each smaller than a grain of sand.

questions.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.note: An octopus has 3 hearts — two pump blood to the gills and one to the rest of the body.

questions.q: How many neck vertebrae does a giraffe have?
questions.note: A giraffe has just 7 neck vertebrae — exactly the same number as a human — each up to 25 cm long.

questions.q: How many compartments does a cow's stomach have?
questions.note: A cow's stomach has 4 compartments, letting it re-chew and slowly ferment tough grass.

questions.q: How many pairs of heart-like organs pump blood around an earthworm's body?
questions.note: An earthworm has 5 pairs of aortic arches, often described as its five hearts.

questions.q: How many spots does the common seven-spot ladybird have?
questions.note: True to its name, the seven-spot ladybird carries exactly 7 spots — three on each wing case and one shared.

questions.q: Through how many degrees can an owl rotate its head?
questions.note: Owls can turn their heads about 270 degrees, thanks to extra vertebrae and special blood vessels.

questions.q: How many chromosomes does a dog have?
questions.note: Dogs have 78 chromosomes in 39 pairs — 32 more than humans.

questions.q: Roughly how many individual muscles make up an elephant's trunk?
questions.note: An elephant's trunk contains about 40,000 muscles; the entire human body has around 600.

questions.q: Roughly how many quills does a North American porcupine carry?
questions.note: A porcupine bristles with about 30,000 quills, each tipped with tiny backward-facing barbs.

questions.q: Roughly how many tiny lenses make up each of a dragonfly's compound eyes?
questions.note: Each eye packs about 30,000 lenses, giving dragonflies nearly all-round vision.

questions.q: Roughly how many teeth does a great white shark have in its mouth at any one time?
questions.note: A great white carries about 300 teeth arranged in rows, with new ones always ready to move forward.

questions.q: How many hairs per square inch does a sea otter's coat pack, the densest fur of any animal?
questions.note: With up to 1,000,000 hairs per square inch, sea otters keep warm without any blubber.

questions.q: How many legs does Eumillipes persephone, the leggiest animal ever found, described in 2021, have?
questions.note: Found deep underground in Australia, it has 1,306 legs — the first true millipede to top a thousand.

questions.q: Roughly how many kilometres does an Arctic tern fly in a year on its pole-to-pole migration?
questions.note: Tracking showed round trips of about 71,000 km a year, the longest migration of any animal.

questions.q: Roughly how many kilometres do monarch butterflies fly from Canada to their winter roosts in Mexico?
questions.note: Monarchs travel about 4,800 km to mountain forests their great-grandparents left months before.

questions.q: How many kilometres did a bar-tailed godwit fly nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania in 2022, a world record?
questions.note: The young godwit flew 13,560 km in 11 days without landing, eating or drinking.

questions.q: At what altitude, in metres, was a Rüppell's vulture recorded in 1973, the highest-flying bird ever documented?
questions.note: The vulture was recorded at 11,300 metres — higher than the summit of Everest and cruising airliners.

questions.q: For how many months can a common swift stay airborne without landing, according to a 2016 tracking study?
questions.note: Swifts can fly for 10 months straight, eating and even sleeping on the wing.

questions.q: How many kilometres did a polar bear swim continuously in the Beaufort Sea, the longest swim recorded for the species?
questions.note: The female swam 687 km over nine days through open water without a rest.

questions.q: Roughly how many times per second does a ruby-throated hummingbird beat its wings in normal flight?
questions.note: At about 50 beats per second, the wings blur into the hum that gives the bird its name.

questions.q: Roughly how many times per second does a honeybee beat its wings?
questions.note: A honeybee's wings beat about 230 times per second, producing its familiar buzz.

questions.q: How many million years ago did the asteroid impact that ended the age of dinosaurs occur?
questions.note: The impact 66 million years ago wiped out three-quarters of species — but birds survived.

questions.q: How many million years ago did the first sharks appear in the oceans?
questions.note: Sharks appeared about 450 million years ago — long before the first trees grew on land.

questions.q: How long is Sue, the famous Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton at Chicago's Field Museum, in metres?
questions.note: Sue stretches 12.3 metres and is the most complete T. rex skeleton ever found.

questions.q: How long is the giant titanosaur skeleton cast displayed at the American Museum of Natural History, in metres?
questions.note: At 37 metres, the Patagotitan cast is too long for its gallery — its head pokes out of the doorway.

questions.q: How long is Dippy, the Natural History Museum's beloved Diplodocus cast, in metres?
questions.note: Dippy measures 21.3 metres and greeted visitors in London's grand Hintze Hall for decades.

questions.q: What is the deepest dive recorded for an emperor penguin, in metres?
questions.note: An emperor penguin has been recorded diving to 564 metres, deeper than any other bird.

questions.q: How deep, in metres, did a Cuvier's beaked whale dive in a 2014 study, the deepest dive recorded for any mammal?
questions.note: The whale reached 2,992 metres — nearly three kilometres straight down.

questions.q: How many litres of water can a thirsty camel drink in around 13 minutes?
questions.note: A dehydrated camel can gulp down 113 litres in about 13 minutes — a bathtub's worth.

questions.q: How many volts can an electric eel discharge in a single shock?
questions.note: An electric eel can deliver about 600 volts, several times the strength of a wall socket.

questions.q: What percentage of their DNA do humans and chimpanzees share?
questions.note: Humans and chimps share about 98.8% of their DNA, making them our closest living relatives.

questions.q: What percentage of a jellyfish's body is water?
questions.note: A jellyfish is about 95% water, which is why one stranded on a beach all but vanishes.

questions.q: What is the lowest temperature, in degrees Celsius, that tardigrades have survived in laboratory tests?
questions.note: Tardigrades have survived about -272 °C, a whisker above absolute zero.

questions.q: In which year was the first complete Archaeopteryx fossil, linking dinosaurs and birds, discovered in Germany?
questions.note: The 1861 find, two years after Darwin's Origin of Species, showed a creature with both feathers and teeth.

questions.q: In which year did Martha, the world's last passenger pigeon, die at Cincinnati Zoo?
questions.note: Martha died in 1914, ending a species that had once darkened American skies in the billions.

questions.q: In which year did the last known thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, die at Hobart Zoo?
questions.note: The last thylacine, remembered as Benjamin, died in 1936, just weeks after the species gained legal protection.

questions.q: In which year was a living coelacanth, a fish thought extinct for 66 million years, caught off South Africa?
questions.source: South African Institute for Aquatic Biodiversity
questions.note: The 1938 catch stunned scientists — a 'living fossil' hauled up in an ordinary trawl net.

questions.q: In which year did the dog Laika become the first animal to orbit the Earth?
questions.note: Laika, a stray from the Moscow streets, orbited Earth aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957.

questions.q: In which year was Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, born?
questions.note: Dolly was born in 1996 in Scotland, named after the singer Dolly Parton.

questions.q: How many seconds long is the longest recorded flight by a chicken?
questions.note: The record chicken flight lasted just 13 seconds — poultry are built for scratching, not soaring.

questions.q: How many species of sea turtle swim in the world's oceans?
questions.note: There are 7 sea turtle species, from the tiny Kemp's ridley to the giant leatherback.

questions.q: How many species of penguin are there in the world?
questions.note: There are 18 penguin species, and several of them live nowhere near Antarctica.

questions.q: Roughly how many species of bat are known worldwide?
questions.note: With about 1,400 species, bats make up roughly one in five of all mammal species.

questions.q: Roughly how many species of butterfly are known worldwide?
questions.note: Around 17,500 butterfly species flutter across every continent except Antarctica.

questions.q: How many species of egg-laying mammal, the monotremes, survive today?
questions.note: Only 5 monotreme species remain: the platypus and four kinds of echidna.

questions.q: How many centimetres can the fastest bamboo grow in a single day?
questions.note: Some bamboo species can grow 91 cm in a day — you could almost watch it happen.

questions.q: About how many teeth did a Tyrannosaurus rex have?
questions.note: Around 60, the largest the size of bananas — and they were replaced throughout its life.

questions.q: How many eggs can a queen honey bee lay in a single day at her peak?
questions.note: Up to 2,000 a day in early summer — more than her own body weight in eggs.

questions.q: How tall is Mount Everest, the world's highest peak, in metres above sea level?
questions.note: The 2020 Nepal-China joint survey settled it at 8,849 metres, snow cap included.

questions.q: How tall is K2, the world's second-highest mountain, in metres?
questions.note: K2 rises to 8,611 metres, just 238 metres shy of Everest yet far deadlier to climb.

questions.q: How tall is Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak, in metres?
questions.note: Kilimanjaro tops out at 5,895 metres and still keeps glaciers just three degrees from the equator.

questions.q: How tall is Mont Blanc, the highest peak in the Alps, in metres?
questions.note: Mont Blanc stands about 4,808 metres, a figure that shifts by a metre or two as its snow cap changes.

questions.q: How tall is Denali, North America's highest mountain, in metres?
questions.note: A 2015 USGS survey put Denali at 6,190 metres, trimming three metres off the old figure.

questions.q: How tall is Aconcagua, the highest mountain in the Americas, in metres?
questions.note: Argentina's Aconcagua reaches 6,961 metres, the tallest peak anywhere outside Asia.

questions.q: How tall is the Matterhorn, the pyramid-shaped peak on the Swiss-Italian border, in metres?
questions.note: The Matterhorn's famous pyramid tops out at 4,478 metres and inspired the Toblerone logo.

questions.q: How tall is Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain, in metres?
questions.note: Mount Fuji rises to 3,776 metres and is climbed by hundreds of thousands of people each summer.

questions.q: How tall is Ben Nevis, the highest mountain in the British Isles, in metres?
questions.note: A 2016 Ordnance Survey re-measurement made Ben Nevis officially 1,345 metres, one metre taller than before.

questions.q: How tall is Mount Kosciuszko, the highest peak on the Australian mainland, in metres?
questions.note: Australia's rooftop is a gentle 2,228 metres — you can walk to the summit on a paved path.

questions.q: How many mountains on Earth are taller than 8,000 metres?
questions.note: There are 14 'eight-thousanders', and every single one stands in the Himalaya or Karakoram ranges.

questions.q: How long is the River Nile, generally counted as the world's longest river, in kilometres?
questions.note: The Nile runs about 6,650 km from its headwaters to the Mediterranean, draining a tenth of Africa.

questions.q: How long is the Amazon River in kilometres?
questions.note: At roughly 6,400 km, the Amazon carries more water than the next seven biggest rivers combined.

questions.q: How long is the Yangtze, Asia's longest river, in kilometres?
questions.note: The Yangtze flows about 6,300 km entirely within one country, China — no other river that long does.

questions.q: Through how many countries does the River Danube flow?
questions.source: International Commission for the Protection of the Danube River
questions.note: The Danube touches 10 countries on its way to the Black Sea, more than any other river on Earth.

questions.q: How long is the River Thames in kilometres?
questions.note: The Thames winds 346 km from a Gloucestershire meadow to the North Sea.

questions.q: How tall is Angel Falls in Venezuela, the world's highest waterfall, in metres?
questions.note: Angel Falls plunges 979 metres — so far that much of the water turns to mist before landing.

questions.q: How tall is Victoria Falls on the Zambezi River in metres?
questions.note: Victoria Falls drops 108 metres, and its spray can be seen from about 50 km away.

questions.q: How long is the Grand Canyon in kilometres?
questions.note: The Grand Canyon stretches 446 km along the Colorado River — roughly the distance from Paris to Amsterdam.

questions.q: How deep is the Challenger Deep, the lowest known point in the ocean, in metres?
questions.note: The Challenger Deep bottoms out around 10,935 metres — Everest would vanish beneath it with room to spare.

questions.q: What is the area of the Pacific Ocean in millions of square kilometres?
questions.note: At about 165 million km², the Pacific covers more of the planet than every continent combined.

questions.q: What percentage of Earth's surface is covered by ocean?
questions.note: Oceans blanket about 71% of the planet, yet more than 80% of them remain unmapped in detail.

questions.q: What is the approximate salt content of the Dead Sea, as a percentage?
questions.note: At roughly 34% salinity — nearly ten times the open ocean — the Dead Sea lets bathers float like corks.

questions.q: How long is Australia's Great Barrier Reef in kilometres?
questions.source: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority
questions.note: The reef system runs about 2,300 km — the largest structure built by living things on Earth.

questions.q: How wide is the Bering Strait between Russia and Alaska at its narrowest, in kilometres?
questions.note: Just 82 km of water separate Asia from North America at the Bering Strait.

questions.q: What is the area of the Sahara Desert in millions of square kilometres?
questions.note: The Sahara sprawls across about 9.2 million km², almost the size of the entire United States.

questions.q: What is the area of Antarctica, the world's largest desert, in millions of square kilometres?
questions.note: Antarctica's 14 million km² of ice count as a desert — its interior gets less precipitation than the Sahara.

questions.q: How many member states does the United Nations have?
questions.note: The UN has counted 193 member states ever since South Sudan joined in 2011.

questions.q: How many countries are there in Africa?
questions.note: Africa's 54 countries make it the continent with the most nations by far.

questions.q: How many independent countries are there in South America?
questions.note: South America has just 12 countries — and only two of them, Bolivia and Paraguay, are landlocked.

questions.q: What is the area of Russia, the world's largest country, in millions of square kilometres?
questions.note: Russia covers about 17.1 million km² — nearly twice the size of the runner-up, Canada.

questions.q: Through how many countries does the equator pass?
questions.note: The equator crosses 13 countries, including Ecuador — which is simply Spanish for 'equator'.

questions.q: How many landlocked countries are there in the world?
questions.note: Some 44 countries have no coastline at all, and two of them are even landlocked by other landlocked countries.

questions.q: How long is Canada's coastline, the longest of any country, in kilometres?
questions.note: Canada's coastline measures a staggering 202,080 km — walking it at 20 km a day would take almost 28 years.

questions.q: How many time zones does Russia span?
questions.note: Russia stretches across 11 time zones — when Kaliningrad sits down to dinner, Kamchatka is eating breakfast.

questions.q: Counting its overseas territories, how many time zones does France use?
questions.note: Thanks to territories from Tahiti to Réunion, France uses 12 time zones — more than any other country.

questions.q: How many official time zones does China use?
questions.note: Despite being about 5,000 km wide, China runs on just 1 official time zone: Beijing time.

questions.q: How long is Chile from north to south, in kilometres?
questions.note: Chile stretches about 4,300 km from desert to glaciers, yet averages only around 180 km wide.

questions.q: How many countries share a land border with China?
questions.note: China borders 14 countries, tying Russia for the most neighbours in the world.

questions.q: How many countries share a land border with Brazil?
questions.note: Brazil borders 10 countries — every South American nation except Chile and Ecuador.

questions.q: What is the area of Vatican City, the world's smallest country, in square kilometres?
questions.note: Vatican City covers just 0.44 km² — you could stroll around the whole country in under an hour.

questions.q: What is the area of Australia in millions of square kilometres?
questions.note: Australia spans about 7.7 million km², making it the only country that covers an entire continent.

questions.q: According to the national mapping agency's count, how many islands make up the Philippines?
questions.note: A 2016 mapping survey counted 7,641 islands in the Philippines — over 500 more than the old figure.

questions.q: How tall is the Eiffel Tower today, including its antennas, in metres?
questions.note: With its broadcast antenna, the Eiffel Tower now stands 330 metres — 18 metres taller than on opening day.

questions.q: How tall is the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, the world's tallest building, in metres?
questions.source: Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat
questions.note: The Burj Khalifa soars 828 metres — its tip can be seen from about 95 km away on a clear day.

questions.q: In which year did the Burj Khalifa officially open?
questions.source: Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat
questions.note: It opened in January 2010 and has held the world height record ever since.

questions.q: How tall is the Statue of Liberty from the ground to the tip of the torch, including its pedestal, in metres?
questions.note: Pedestal included, Lady Liberty reaches 93 metres; the copper statue itself is only 46.

questions.q: In which year was the Statue of Liberty dedicated in New York Harbor?
questions.note: France's gift was dedicated in 1886, and its copper skin took about 30 years to turn green.

questions.q: According to China's 2012 national survey, how long is the Great Wall of China in kilometres?
questions.note: The 2012 survey measured 21,196 km of wall in total — more than half the circumference of the Earth.

questions.q: How long is the main span of the Golden Gate Bridge in metres?
questions.note: Its main span stretches 1,280 metres, a world record it held for 27 years after 1937.

questions.q: In which year did the Sydney Harbour Bridge open?
questions.note: The 'Coathanger' opened in 1932 after nine years of construction and 6 million rivets.

questions.q: How long is the Panama Canal in kilometres?
questions.note: The canal cuts just 82 km across the isthmus, saving ships a 13,000 km voyage around South America.

questions.q: In which year did the Panama Canal open to shipping?
questions.note: It opened in 1914, just as the First World War began, so the fanfare was rather muted.

questions.q: In which year did the Suez Canal open?
questions.note: The Suez Canal opened in 1869 after a decade of digging, instantly shortening the Europe-Asia route by weeks.

questions.q: How long is the Channel Tunnel between England and France in kilometres?
questions.note: The tunnel runs just over 50 km, and 38 of them are bored beneath the seabed.

questions.q: In which year did the Channel Tunnel open?
questions.note: It opened in 1994, realising an idea first seriously proposed to Napoleon in 1802.

questions.q: How tall is the Elizabeth Tower, home of Big Ben, in metres?
questions.note: The tower rises 96 metres; strictly speaking, 'Big Ben' is only the 13.7-tonne bell inside it.

questions.q: How tall is the Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, excluding its pedestal, in metres?
questions.note: The statue itself is 30 metres tall, with arms stretching 28 metres from fingertip to fingertip.

questions.q: How tall was the Great Pyramid of Giza when it was completed, in metres?
questions.note: It originally rose 146.6 metres and remained the world's tallest structure for over 3,800 years.

questions.q: At what altitude above sea level does Machu Picchu sit, in metres?
questions.note: The Inca citadel perches at 2,430 metres, wrapped in cloud forest on a ridge above the Urubamba River.

questions.q: How tall is the Taj Mahal, from its base to the top of its dome finial, in metres?
questions.note: The marble mausoleum rises 73 metres and appears to change colour from dawn to dusk.

questions.q: How tall is each carved presidential head on Mount Rushmore, in metres?
questions.note: Each face is about 18 metres tall — the same height as a six-storey building.

questions.q: How tall is Toronto's CN Tower in metres?
questions.note: At 553 metres, the CN Tower was the world's tallest free-standing structure for 32 years.

questions.q: How tall is the Empire State Building to its roof, excluding the antenna, in metres?
questions.note: The 1931 skyscraper rises 381 metres to the roof and was built in a remarkable 410 days.

questions.q: How tall is the Hoover Dam in metres?
questions.note: The dam stands 221 metres high, and its concrete is still slowly curing nearly a century on.

questions.q: How tall is China's Three Gorges Dam in metres?
questions.note: The dam wall rises 185 metres and holds back a reservoir stretching some 600 km upstream.

questions.q: How long is the main span of Japan's Akashi Kaikyo Bridge, the world's longest when it opened in 1998, in metres?
questions.note: Its 1,991-metre span was stretched a full metre by the 1995 Kobe earthquake during construction.

questions.q: How tall is the tallest mast of the Millau Viaduct in France, in metres?
questions.note: At 343 metres, the Millau Viaduct's tallest mast overtops the Eiffel Tower.

questions.q: How tall is the Tokyo Skytree in metres?
questions.note: Its 634-metre height was chosen because the digits 6-3-4 can be read 'Musashi', an old name for the region.

questions.q: In which year did the Sydney Opera House open?
questions.note: It opened in 1973, ten years late and more than fourteen times over budget — now a UNESCO icon.

questions.q: In which year did Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay make the first confirmed ascent of Mount Everest?
questions.note: They reached the summit on 29 May 1953, and news arrived in London on the morning of the Queen's coronation.

questions.q: How long is the Trans-Siberian Railway from Moscow to Vladivostok, in kilometres?
questions.note: The full 9,289 km journey crosses seven time zones and takes about a week without stopovers.

questions.q: Roughly how many basalt columns make up the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland?
questions.note: About 40,000 interlocking columns formed as lava cooled 60 million years ago, most of them neat hexagons.

questions.q: What is the area of Greenland, the world's largest island, in millions of square kilometres?
questions.note: Greenland spans about 2.17 million km², yet around 80% of it lies under a permanent ice sheet.

questions.q: What is the area of Madagascar, the world's fourth-largest island, in square kilometres?
questions.note: Madagascar covers about 587,000 km², and roughly 90% of its wildlife exists nowhere else.

questions.q: How deep is Lake Baikal in Siberia, the world's deepest lake, in metres?
questions.note: Baikal plunges 1,642 metres and holds about a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on Earth.

questions.q: What is the area of the Caspian Sea, the world's largest inland body of water, in square kilometres?
questions.note: At about 371,000 km², the Caspian is bigger than Germany, yet it is technically a lake.

questions.q: At what altitude does Lake Titicaca sit, in metres above sea level?
questions.note: At 3,812 metres, Titicaca is the highest large navigable lake in the world.

questions.q: How deep is Crater Lake in Oregon, the deepest lake in the United States, in metres?
questions.note: Crater Lake reaches 594 metres deep inside a collapsed volcano, filled only by rain and snow.

questions.q: In which year did the volcanic island of Surtsey erupt out of the sea off Iceland?
questions.note: Surtsey rose from the Atlantic in 1963 and has been a protected natural laboratory ever since.

questions.q: At what altitude does La Paz, Bolivia's seat of government, sit in metres above sea level?
questions.note: At about 3,640 metres, La Paz is the world's highest seat of national government — visitors often need days to acclimatise.

questions.q: At what latitude, in degrees north, does Reykjavik sit as the world's northernmost capital city?
questions.note: Reykjavik lies at about 64°N, where midsummer nights never get fully dark.

questions.q: How far below sea level is Badwater Basin in Death Valley, the lowest point in North America, in metres?
questions.note: Badwater Basin sits 86 metres below sea level, barely 140 km from 4,400-metre Mount Whitney.

questions.q: What is the highest air temperature ever reliably recorded on Earth, measured in Death Valley in 1913, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Furnace Creek hit 56.7°C in July 1913, a record the WMO still recognises as the world's hottest.

questions.q: What is the coldest temperature ever recorded at ground level on Earth, at Vostok Station in Antarctica in 1983, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Vostok Station registered -89.2°C in 1983 — cold enough for steel to shatter like glass.

questions.q: What is the circumference of the Earth around the equator, in kilometres?
questions.note: Earth measures 40,075 km around the equator — about 67 km more than around the poles, because it bulges.

questions.q: At approximately what latitude, in degrees north, does the Tropic of Cancer lie?
questions.note: The Tropic of Cancer sits near 23.4°N, marking the northernmost point where the sun can be directly overhead.

questions.q: How fast is the Atlantic Ocean widening each year, in centimetres?
questions.note: The Atlantic grows about 2.5 cm a year — roughly the speed at which your fingernails grow.

questions.q: What percentage of the world's fresh water is locked up in the Antarctic ice sheet?
questions.source: National Snow and Ice Data Center
questions.note: About 70% of Earth's fresh water sits frozen in Antarctica's ice sheet.

questions.q: What percentage of the world's active volcanoes are found along the Pacific Ring of Fire?
questions.note: About 75% of Earth's active volcanoes ring the Pacific, along with most of its big earthquakes.

questions.q: How long is the Andes, the world's longest mountain range on land, in kilometres?
questions.note: The Andes run about 8,900 km down South America's western edge, through seven countries.

questions.q: How high does Uluru rise above the surrounding Australian desert plain, in metres?
questions.note: Uluru rises 348 metres above the plain, but like an iceberg, most of the rock continues far underground.

questions.q: What is the average natural ground elevation of the Maldives, the world's lowest-lying country, in metres above sea level?
questions.note: The Maldives average just 1.5 metres above the sea — the flattest, lowest country on Earth.

questions.q: What percentage of the Netherlands lies below sea level?
questions.note: About 26% of the Netherlands sits below sea level, kept dry by dunes, dykes and pumps.

questions.q: In which year was Yellowstone established as the world's first national park?
questions.note: Yellowstone became the world's first national park in 1872, decades before the US had an agency to run it.

questions.q: How high above sea level is the summit of Mauna Kea in Hawaii, in metres?
questions.note: Mauna Kea's summit stands 4,207 metres above the sea, but measured from its ocean-floor base it exceeds 10,000 metres.

questions.q: How long is the Suez Canal in kilometres?
questions.note: After its 2015 expansion the Suez Canal runs 193 km, linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea with no locks at all.

questions.q: How deep is Loch Ness at its deepest point, in metres?
questions.note: About 227 m — Loch Ness holds more water than every lake in England and Wales combined.

questions.q: Roughly what percentage of all the river water that flows into the world's oceans comes from the Amazon?
questions.note: About 20% — more than the next seven biggest rivers combined.

questions.q: What is the surface area of Lake Superior, the world's largest freshwater lake by area, in square kilometres?
questions.note: 82,100 km² — larger than Austria.

questions.q: In which year AD did Mount Vesuvius erupt and bury the Roman town of Pompeii?
questions.note: Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, sealing Pompeii under ash so completely that loaves of bread were later found still in their ovens.
