questions.note: 32 acts played across three days, with Jimi Hendrix closing to a dwindling Monday-morning crowd.

questions.q: How many pounds did a ticket to the first Glastonbury Festival in 1970 cost?
questions.note: Entry cost just 1 pound and included free milk from the farm.

questions.q: In which year did the Live Aid concerts take place in London and Philadelphia?
questions.note: Live Aid spanned two continents in 1985 and was watched by well over a billion people.

questions.q: How many countries competed in the first Eurovision Song Contest in 1956?
questions.note: Just 7 countries took part in Lugano in 1956, with host nation Switzerland winning.

questions.q: In which year did ABBA win Eurovision with Waterloo?
questions.note: ABBA's 1974 victory in Brighton launched the most successful career Eurovision has ever produced.

questions.q: In which year did Celine Dion win the Eurovision Song Contest for Switzerland?
questions.note: A 20-year-old Celine Dion won for Switzerland in 1988 by a single point.

questions.q: How many strings does a violin have?
questions.note: The violin's 4 strings are tuned in fifths: G, D, A and E.

questions.q: How many keys does a full-size piano have?
questions.note: The modern piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.

questions.q: How many strings does a standard guitar have?
questions.note: The standard guitar carries 6 strings, tuned E, A, D, G, B, E.

questions.q: How many strings does a full-size concert harp have?
questions.note: A concert pedal harp has 47 strings spanning six and a half octaves.

questions.q: How many strings does a mandolin have?
questions.note: The mandolin's 8 strings are arranged in four doubled pairs, giving its shimmering sound.

questions.q: How many valves does a standard trumpet have?
questions.note: Just 3 valves, in combination, give the trumpet its full chromatic range.

questions.q: How many slide positions does a trombone have?
questions.note: The trombone slide has 7 positions, each lowering the pitch by a semitone.

questions.q: How many drone pipes does a Great Highland bagpipe have?
questions.note: The Highland pipes carry 3 drones: two tenors and one bass, humming beneath the melody.

questions.q: How many pieces make up a standard rock drum kit?
questions.note: The classic kit has 5 pieces: bass drum, snare, two toms and a floor tom, plus cymbals on top.

questions.q: Approximately how many strings are inside a full-size grand piano?
questions.note: About 230 strings, under some 20 tonnes of combined tension, hide behind those 88 keys.

questions.q: In which year did Adolphe Sax patent the saxophone?
questions.note: The Belgian inventor patented his saxophone in 1846, decades before jazz made it famous.

questions.q: In which year did Antonio Stradivari craft his famous Messiah violin?
questions.note: Made in 1716 during Stradivari's golden period, the Messiah remains in almost unplayed condition.

questions.q: Around which year did Bartolomeo Cristofori build the first piano?
questions.note: Cristofori had built his first piano by around 1700, calling it a harpsichord that plays soft and loud.

questions.q: Roughly how many years old are the bone flutes found in German caves, the world's oldest known musical instruments?
questions.note: The bird-bone and ivory flutes are roughly 40,000 years old, older than the last Ice Age's peak.

questions.q: How long is a Steinway Model D concert grand piano in metres?
questions.note: The Model D stretches 2.74 metres, the standard concert grand on the world's great stages.

questions.q: In which year did Fender introduce the Stratocaster electric guitar?
questions.note: The 1954 Stratocaster became the world's most copied guitar shape, beloved by Hendrix and Clapton alike.

questions.q: Standard concert pitch tunes the note A above middle C to how many hertz?
questions.note: A at 440 Hz was fixed as the international standard in 1955, and orchestras tune to it daily.

questions.q: How many semitones make up an octave in Western music?
questions.note: The octave divides into 12 semitones, the full set of notes on a piano from C to B.

questions.q: How many lines are in a standard musical staff?
questions.note: Written music has sat on a 5-line staff since around the 16th century.

questions.q: How many syllables make up the do-re-mi solfege scale?
questions.note: The 7 syllables run do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti, as The Sound of Music taught the world.

questions.q: In which year did Johann Maelzel patent the metronome?
questions.note: Maelzel patented the ticking timekeeper in 1815, and Beethoven was among the first to use it.

questions.q: How many seconds of silence make up John Cage's composition 4'33"?
questions.note: The piece lasts exactly 273 seconds, in which the only music is the sound of the room itself.

questions.q: How many pedals does a modern grand piano have?
questions.note: The modern grand has 3 pedals: sustain, sostenuto and una corda.

questions.q: How many symphonies did Beethoven complete?
questions.note: Beethoven completed 9 symphonies, and the superstition of a ninth-symphony curse haunted composers after him.

questions.q: How many piano sonatas did Beethoven compose?
questions.note: His 32 piano sonatas, including the Moonlight, are often called the pianist's New Testament.

questions.q: How many operas did Beethoven compose?
questions.note: Beethoven wrote just 1 opera, Fidelio, though he revised it obsessively for a decade.

questions.q: In which year was Ludwig van Beethoven born?
questions.note: Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, the same city that now houses his museum.

questions.q: How many notes form the famous opening motif of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony?
questions.note: The 4-note da-da-da-dum is often described as fate knocking at the door.

questions.q: How many numbered symphonies did Mozart compose?
questions.note: Mozart's 41 numbered symphonies end with the Jupiter, written when he was just 32.

questions.q: How many works are numbered in the Koechel catalogue of Mozart's music?
questions.note: The catalogue runs to K. 626, which is the unfinished Requiem Mozart left at his death.

questions.q: At what age did Mozart write his first symphony?
questions.note: Mozart wrote his first symphony at 8, while touring London with his family.

questions.q: At what age did Mozart die?
questions.note: Mozart died at just 35, leaving over 600 works and an unfinished Requiem.

questions.q: How many numbered symphonies did Joseph Haydn compose?
questions.note: The Father of the Symphony wrote 104 of them, more than Mozart and Beethoven combined.

questions.q: How many Brandenburg Concertos did Bach compose?
questions.note: Bach presented 6 Brandenburg Concertos to a margrave who probably never had them performed.

questions.q: How many variations make up Bach's Goldberg Variations?
questions.note: The work spins one gentle aria into 30 variations before the aria returns to close the circle.

questions.q: How many children did Johann Sebastian Bach father?
questions.note: Bach fathered 20 children, four of whom became notable composers themselves.

questions.q: In which year was Johann Sebastian Bach born?
questions.note: Bach was born in 1685, the same year as Handel and Domenico Scarlatti.

questions.q: How many symphonies did Johannes Brahms compose?
questions.note: Brahms wrote only 4 symphonies, taking over 20 years to dare finish his first.

questions.q: How many preludes are in Chopin's Opus 28?
questions.note: The 24 preludes visit every major and minor key, including the famous Raindrop.

questions.q: How many violin concertos make up Vivaldi's The Four Seasons?
questions.note: The 4 concertos each come with a sonnet describing their season, possibly written by Vivaldi himself.

questions.q: How many movements are in Holst's orchestral suite The Planets?
questions.note: The Planets has 7 movements, one for each planet known then except Earth itself.

questions.q: How many movements are in Saint-Saens' The Carnival of the Animals?
questions.note: The 14 movements include The Swan and a teasing portrait of pianists as animals.

questions.q: How many cannon shots does the score of Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture call for?
questions.note: The score demands 16 cannon shots, which concert halls usually fake and outdoor festivals gleefully fire.

questions.q: In roughly how many days did Handel compose the entire Messiah oratorio?
questions.note: Handel wrote the whole of Messiah in about 24 days of feverish work in 1741.

questions.q: In which year did Johann Strauss II premiere The Blue Danube waltz?
questions.note: The Blue Danube debuted in 1867 and is now Austria's unofficial anthem, played every New Year in Vienna.

questions.q: Roughly how many performers took part in the 1910 premiere of Mahler's Symphony of a Thousand?
questions.note: About 1,030 singers and players crowded the Munich stage, earning the symphony its nickname.

questions.q: How many completed movements does Schubert's Unfinished Symphony have?
questions.note: Schubert completed only 2 movements, and nobody knows why he set the symphony aside.

questions.q: Approximately how many hours does Wagner's complete Ring cycle take to perform?
questions.note: The four operas of the Ring run about 15 hours, usually spread across four evenings.

questions.q: How many roof tiles cover the sails of the Sydney Opera House?
questions.note: Exactly 1,056,006 Swedish-made tiles cover the sails, and they are self-cleaning in the rain.

questions.q: How many people can the Royal Albert Hall seat?
questions.note: The circular hall seats 5,272 people beneath its great glass dome, home of the Proms since 1941.

questions.q: Roughly how many musicians play in a full symphony orchestra?
questions.note: A full symphony orchestra fields around 100 musicians, more than half of them string players.

questions.q: In which year did Monteverdi premiere L'Orfeo, the earliest opera still widely performed?
questions.note: L'Orfeo premiered in Mantua in 1607 and still holds the stage more than four centuries on.

questions.q: How many numbered symphonies did Tchaikovsky complete?
questions.note: Tchaikovsky completed 6 symphonies, conducting the premiere of the Pathetique days before his death.

questions.q: How many tracks are on Miles Davis's landmark album Kind of Blue?
questions.note: Just 5 tracks, largely improvised in two sessions in 1959, became the best-selling jazz album ever.

questions.q: In which year were the first modern Olympic Games held in Athens?
questions.note: Pierre de Coubertin's revived Games opened in Athens in 1896, with 241 athletes and not a single woman among them.

questions.q: How many interlocking rings appear on the Olympic flag?
questions.note: The 5 rings represent the five inhabited continents, and every national flag on Earth contains at least one of the six colours used.

questions.q: In which year were the first Winter Olympic Games held in Chamonix, France?
questions.note: The 1924 Chamonix Games were only retroactively declared the first Winter Olympics — at the time they were billed as an 'International Winter Sports Week'.

questions.q: In which year did Tokyo first host the Summer Olympic Games?
questions.note: Tokyo 1964 was the first Olympics held in Asia, and Japan unveiled its bullet train just days before the opening ceremony.

questions.q: How many Olympic gold medals did swimmer Michael Phelps win across his career?
questions.note: Phelps retired with 23 golds — more than most countries have won in their entire Olympic history.

questions.q: How many gold medals did Michael Phelps win at the 2008 Beijing Olympics alone?
questions.note: Phelps took 8 golds in Beijing, beating Mark Spitz's single-Games record of seven that had stood since 1972.

questions.q: In which year did gymnast Nadia Comaneci score the first perfect 10 in Olympic history?
questions.note: In Montreal in 1976 the scoreboard could not display 10.00, so Comaneci's perfect score flashed up as 1.00.

questions.q: How many gold medals did Jesse Owens win at the 1936 Berlin Olympics?
questions.note: Owens won 4 golds in Berlin — the 100m, 200m, long jump and 4x100m relay — inside a single week.

questions.q: How long is an Olympic swimming pool?
questions.note: An Olympic pool is exactly 50 metres long, which is why swimmers call long-course racing 'the honest pool'.

questions.q: As of the 2024 Games, how many times has London hosted the Summer Olympics?
questions.note: London has hosted 3 times — 1908, 1948 and 2012 — more than any other city.

questions.q: In which year were the Winter Olympics first held on a separate cycle from the Summer Games, at Lillehammer?
questions.note: Lillehammer 1994 came just two years after Albertville 1992, shifting winter and summer Games onto alternating even years.

questions.q: What is the minimum amount of pure gold an Olympic gold medal must contain?
questions.note: A 'gold' medal is mostly silver — the rules require only 6 grams of gold, applied as plating.

questions.q: How far did Bob Beamon leap in his famous long jump at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics?
questions.note: Beamon's 8.90 m jump was so far beyond the optical measuring rail that officials had to find a tape measure.

questions.q: For how many years did Bob Beamon's 1968 long jump world record stand?
questions.note: The record survived 23 years until Mike Powell jumped 8.95 m at the 1991 Tokyo World Championships.

questions.q: In which year was the Olympic torch relay first staged?
questions.note: The torch relay debuted in 1936, carrying a flame from Olympia in Greece all the way to Berlin.

questions.q: In which year was the women's marathon first run at the Olympics?
questions.note: Women first raced the Olympic marathon in 1984 in Los Angeles, where Joan Benoit won by well over a minute.

questions.q: In which year was the first FIFA World Cup held in Uruguay?
questions.note: Hosts Uruguay won the inaugural 1930 tournament and declared a national holiday the next day.

questions.q: How many national teams competed at the first World Cup in 1930?
questions.note: Just 13 teams entered in 1930, and three of the four European sides crossed the Atlantic together on the steamship Conte Verde.

questions.q: As of the 2022 tournament, how many World Cups has Brazil won?
questions.note: Brazil's 5 titles make them the only nation to have played in every single World Cup.

questions.q: How wide is a full-size football goal?
questions.note: The goal is 7.32 m wide — the metric echo of the original 8 yards laid down in the 19th century.

questions.q: How high is the crossbar of a full-size football goal?
questions.note: The crossbar sits 2.44 m up — exactly 8 feet, unchanged since crossbars replaced tape in 1882.

questions.q: How far is the penalty spot from the goal line in football?
questions.note: The spot is 11 m out — 12 yards — a distance that gives well-struck penalties under half a second of flight.

questions.q: What is the radius of the centre circle on a football pitch?
questions.note: The centre circle's 9.15 m radius is the same 10-yard distance defenders must retreat at free kicks.

questions.q: How many minutes does a standard football match last, excluding stoppage and extra time?
questions.note: The 90-minute match dates from an 1866 agreement between London and Sheffield clubs who couldn't agree on much else.

questions.q: How many players does each football team field at kick-off?
questions.note: Eleven a side became standard in the 1870s, possibly because school dormitories held ten pupils and a master.

questions.q: In which year was FIFA, football's world governing body, founded in Paris?
questions.note: FIFA began in 1904 with seven European nations; England, football's birthplace, didn't bother to join until the following year.

questions.q: In which year did England win the FIFA World Cup on home soil?
questions.note: England beat West Germany 4-2 at Wembley in 1966 — still their only World Cup triumph.

questions.q: How many goals did Geoff Hurst score in the 1966 World Cup final?
questions.note: Hurst's 3 goals made him the first man to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final, a feat matched only by Kylian Mbappe in 2022.

questions.q: How many World Cup goals did Miroslav Klose score, the all-time record as of 2022?
questions.note: Klose's 16 goals came across four tournaments, and he celebrated many of them with a front flip.

questions.q: How many teams contested each World Cup finals from 1998 to 2022?
questions.note: The 32-team format ran for seven tournaments before expanding to 48 for 2026.

questions.q: In which year did Diego Maradona captain Argentina to World Cup victory in Mexico?
questions.note: In 1986 Maradona scored both the 'Hand of God' and the 'Goal of the Century' in the same quarter-final against England.

questions.q: How many World Cups did Pele win as a player?
questions.note: Pele's 3 wins — 1958, 1962 and 1970 — remain unmatched by any other player.

questions.q: How many Grand Slam tennis tournaments are played each year?
questions.note: The 4 majors — Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon and the US Open — span three different court surfaces.

questions.q: In which year was the first Wimbledon Championship held?
questions.note: The 1877 tournament drew 22 entrants and about 200 spectators, who each paid a shilling for the final.

questions.q: How long is a tennis court from baseline to baseline?
questions.note: A court is 23.77 m long — the metric version of the original 78 feet.

questions.q: How high is a tennis net at its centre?
questions.note: The net dips to 91.4 cm (3 feet) in the middle, which is why so many serves are aimed straight down the centre.

questions.q: Roughly how many hours did the record 2010 Wimbledon match between John Isner and Nicolas Mahut last?
questions.note: The match ran 11 hours 5 minutes over three days, with Isner finally taking the fifth set 70-68.

questions.q: How many Wimbledon singles titles did Roger Federer win in his career?
questions.note: Federer's 8 titles are the most by any man at Wimbledon, five of them won back to back.

questions.q: How many Grand Slam singles titles did Margaret Court win, the most by any woman in history?
questions.note: Court's 24 majors include a calendar-year Grand Slam in 1970, and no woman has matched her total since.

questions.q: In which year did tennis's Open Era begin, allowing professionals into the Grand Slams?
questions.note: From 1968 professionals could finally enter the majors; Rod Laver promptly won Wimbledon as a pro.

questions.q: In which year did Steffi Graf win all four Grand Slams plus Olympic gold — the 'Golden Slam'?
questions.note: Graf's 1988 Golden Slam has never been repeated in singles by any player, man or woman.

questions.q: How many consecutive Wimbledon titles did Bjorn Borg win from 1976 to 1980?
questions.note: Borg took 5 straight titles and then, remarkably, retired from the tour at just 26.

questions.q: As of 2024, how many French Open singles titles had Rafael Nadal won?
questions.note: Nadal's 14 Roland-Garros titles came from just 14 finals — he never lost one — and earned him a statue at the grounds.

questions.q: How wide is a tennis court for singles play?
questions.note: The singles court is 8.23 m wide; the doubles alleys add another 1.37 m to guard on each side.

questions.q: How long is a cricket pitch between the two sets of stumps?
questions.note: The pitch is 22 yards — an old surveyor's 'chain' — a length unchanged since the 1700s.

questions.q: How many overs does each side face in a One Day International cricket match?
questions.note: The 50-over format settled in the 1980s and decides the Cricket World Cup to this day.

questions.q: How many overs does each side face in a Twenty20 cricket match?
questions.note: T20's 20 overs a side squeeze a whole match into about three hours, and the format conquered world cricket within a decade of its 2003 debut.

questions.q: How many legal deliveries make up one over in cricket?
questions.note: An over is 6 balls, though Australia experimented with eight-ball overs for decades before falling into line in 1979.

questions.q: What was Don Bradman's famous Test cricket batting average?
questions.note: Bradman needed just four runs in his final innings to average 100, but was bowled for a duck and finished on 99.94.

questions.q: In which year was the first Cricket World Cup held in England?
questions.note: The 1975 tournament was won by the West Indies, with every match played in whites with a red ball.

questions.q: Over how many days is a Test cricket match scheduled?
questions.note: Tests run up to 5 days and can still end in a draw — a concept that bewilders newcomers to the sport.

questions.q: What is the highest individual score in Test cricket, made by Brian Lara in 2004?
questions.note: Lara's unbeaten 400 against England reclaimed the record he had first set a decade earlier.

questions.q: How tall are cricket stumps, measured above the ground?
questions.note: Stumps stand 71 cm high — 28 inches in the Laws — and the bails resting on top weigh just a few grams each.

questions.q: How many players does a rugby union team have on the field?
questions.note: Union fields 15 a side — eight forwards and seven backs — plus a bench of replacements.

questions.q: How many players does a rugby league team have on the field?
questions.note: League plays 13 a side, having shed two forwards after the codes split in 1895.

questions.q: In which year was the first Rugby World Cup held?
questions.note: New Zealand won the inaugural 1987 tournament, co-hosted with Australia, beating France in the final.

questions.q: How many points is a try worth in rugby union?
questions.note: A try has been worth 5 points since 1992 — in the 19th century it was worth nothing except the right to 'try' a kick.

questions.q: As of the 2023 tournament, how many Rugby World Cups has South Africa won?
questions.note: The Springboks' 4 titles — 1995, 2007, 2019 and 2023 — are the most of any nation.

questions.q: How many minutes does a rugby union match last?
questions.note: Rugby's 80 minutes are split into two halves, with the clock famously allowed to run past time until the ball goes dead.

questions.q: According to legend, in which year did William Webb Ellis pick up the ball at Rugby School and run with it?
questions.note: The 1823 story is almost certainly myth, yet the World Cup trophy is still named the Webb Ellis Cup.

questions.q: In what time did Usain Bolt run the 100 metres world record in Berlin in 2009?
questions.note: Bolt's 9.58 seconds took a startling 0.11 off his own record and has not been approached since.

questions.q: In what time did Usain Bolt set the 200 metres world record in 2009?
questions.note: Bolt clocked 19.19 in Berlin just days after his 100m record, averaging over 37 km/h around the bend.

questions.q: What is the official distance of a marathon?
questions.note: The odd 42.195 km comes from the 1908 London Olympics, when the course was stretched so the race could finish in front of the royal box.

questions.q: In which year did Roger Bannister run the first sub-four-minute mile?
questions.note: Bannister's 3:59.4 in Oxford in 1954 broke a barrier many thought physically impossible — and his record lasted just 46 days.

questions.q: How high is the men's high jump world record, set by Javier Sotomayor in 1993?
questions.note: Sotomayor's 2.45 m — clearing well above his own head — has stood longer than any other men's jumping record.

questions.q: How long is one lap of a standard outdoor athletics track?
questions.note: A lap is 400 m in lane one; run in lane eight and each circuit is over 50 m longer, hence staggered starts.

questions.q: How many hurdles does each athlete clear in the 110 metres hurdles?
questions.note: Sprinters clear 10 hurdles, each 1.067 m high, in a race the best finish in under 13 seconds.

questions.q: How many events make up the decathlon?
questions.note: The decathlon's 10 events unfold over two days, ending with a lung-busting 1500 m.

questions.q: How much does the men's shot weigh in shot put?
questions.note: The men's shot weighs 7.26 kg — a metric relic of the old imperial 16 pounds.

questions.q: In what time did Florence Griffith-Joyner set the women's 100 metres world record in 1988?
questions.note: Flo-Jo's 10.49 from 1988 still stands as the world record — no woman has come within four hundredths of it since.

questions.q: In which year did Eliud Kipchoge run the first sub-two-hour marathon in a special exhibition event?
questions.note: Kipchoge's 1:59:40 in Vienna in 2019 used rotating pacemakers, so it stands as a milestone rather than an official record.

questions.q: In which year did Sergey Bubka become the first pole vaulter to clear six metres?
questions.note: Bubka first cleared 6.00 m in Paris in 1985 and went on to break the world record 35 times.

questions.q: Over what distance is the Olympic steeplechase run?
questions.note: The 3000 m steeplechase includes 28 barriers and 7 water jumps, a format borrowed from cross-country horse racing.

questions.q: In which year was the first Tour de France held?
questions.note: The 1903 Tour was dreamed up to sell newspapers, and its six giant stages averaged over 400 km each.

questions.q: How many stages make up a modern Tour de France?
questions.note: The modern Tour runs 21 stages over three weeks, with just two rest days for tired legs.

questions.q: How many Tour de France general classifications did Eddy Merckx win?
questions.note: Merckx won 5 Tours, and in 1969 he took the yellow, green and polka-dot jerseys all at once — a feat never repeated.

questions.q: In which year was the yellow jersey introduced to the Tour de France?
questions.note: The maillot jaune arrived in 1919, coloured yellow to match the newsprint of the organising paper L'Auto.

questions.q: How many individual Tour de France stage wins did Eddy Merckx take during his career?
questions.note: Merckx's 34 stage wins set a benchmark that stood alone for nearly half a century.

questions.q: Since 2018, how many riders does each team start with in the Tour de France?
questions.note: Teams were trimmed from nine riders to 8 in 2018 to make racing safer and less controlled.

questions.q: How many holes are played in a standard round of golf?
questions.note: The 18-hole round became the world standard because that was the layout at St Andrews.

questions.q: In which year was the first Open Championship played at Prestwick, Scotland?
questions.note: The 1860 Open had just eight professionals playing three loops of a 12-hole course in a single day.

questions.q: How many major championships did Jack Nicklaus win, the men's golf record?
questions.note: Nicklaus's 18 majors span a quarter of a century, the last coming at the 1986 Masters when he was 46.

questions.q: What is the diameter of a golf hole?
questions.note: The hole is 108 mm (4.25 inches) across — the size of the pipe a Musselburgh greenkeeper used as a cutter in 1829.

questions.q: What is the maximum permitted weight of a golf ball?
questions.note: A golf ball may weigh no more than 45.93 g — 1.62 ounces — a limit shared by the R&A and USGA rules.

questions.q: In which year was the first Masters Tournament held at Augusta National?
questions.note: The first Masters in 1934 was billed as the 'Augusta National Invitation Tournament'; the grander name stuck five years later.

questions.q: By how many strokes did Tiger Woods win his record-breaking 1997 Masters?
questions.note: Woods won by 12 shots at age 21, the largest margin in Masters history, in his first major as a professional.

questions.q: In which year did St Andrews reduce its Old Course to the now-standard 18 holes?
questions.note: In 1764 St Andrews merged its first four short holes into two, and golf's 18-hole round was born by accident.

questions.q: In which year did James Naismith invent basketball at a YMCA in Springfield, Massachusetts?
questions.source: Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame
questions.note: Naismith nailed up two peach baskets in 1891 and wrote 13 rules — someone had to fetch the ball after every score.

questions.q: How high above the floor is a basketball hoop?
questions.note: The rim sits at 3.05 m — 10 feet — the height of the running track railing Naismith first hung his baskets from.

questions.q: How many players does each basketball team have on court?
questions.note: Basketball settled on 5 a side in 1897, after early games had featured as many as nine per team.

questions.q: How many seconds does a team have to attempt a shot under the NBA shot clock?
questions.note: The 24-second clock arrived in 1954 to end stalling, and it revived the league almost overnight.

questions.q: How many points did Wilt Chamberlain score in a single NBA game in 1962, the all-time record?
questions.note: Chamberlain's 100-point game in Hershey, Pennsylvania was never televised, and no film of it exists.

questions.q: In which year did the NBA introduce the three-point line?
questions.note: The arc arrived for the 1979-80 season, borrowed from the defunct ABA, and was initially dismissed as a gimmick.

questions.q: What is the inside diameter of a basketball rim?
questions.note: The rim's 45.7 cm (18 inch) opening is nearly twice the diameter of the ball itself, which is why clean swishes are possible at all.

questions.q: How many squares are there on a chessboard?
questions.note: The board's 64 squares have hosted the same starting position since the modern queen's powers were settled around 1500.

questions.q: How many pieces does each chess player start with?
questions.note: Each side begins with 16 — eight pawns and eight pieces — and a full board holds half its squares occupied.

questions.q: How many pawns does each player have at the start of a chess game?
questions.note: The 8 pawns were called the 'soul of chess' by 18th-century champion Philidor, and any one can become a queen.

questions.q: In which year did IBM's Deep Blue computer defeat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match?
questions.note: Deep Blue's 1997 win was the first match defeat of a reigning world champion by a machine, examining up to 200 million positions a second.

questions.q: In which year was the first official World Chess Championship match played?
questions.note: Wilhelm Steinitz beat Johannes Zukertort in 1886 to become the first official world champion.

questions.q: In which year did Bobby Fischer win the world chess championship in Reykjavik?
questions.note: Fischer's 1972 victory over Boris Spassky was dubbed the Match of the Century and made chess front-page news worldwide.

questions.q: In which year did Ray Kroc open his first McDonald's franchise in Des Plaines, Illinois?
questions.note: Kroc opened his Des Plaines restaurant in 1955, and its first day's takings came to just $366.12.

questions.q: In which year did pharmacist John Pemberton first serve Coca-Cola in Atlanta?
questions.note: Pemberton poured the first Coca-Cola at Jacobs' Pharmacy in 1886, selling around nine glasses a day.

questions.q: In which year does Nestlé date its founding, with the Anglo-Swiss Condensed Milk Company?
questions.note: Nestlé traces its story to 1866, before Henri Nestlé's infant cereal joined the family the following year.

questions.q: In which year did the first Starbucks open near Pike Place Market in Seattle?
questions.note: The original 1971 Starbucks sold only whole roasted beans — you could not buy a cup of coffee there.

questions.q: In which year was the Oreo cookie first sold?
questions.note: The first Oreos left the Chelsea factory in New York in 1912, and the design has barely aged a day.

questions.q: In which year did Ferrero launch Nutella under that name?
questions.note: Nutella got its name in 1964, evolving from a wartime paste that stretched scarce cocoa with plentiful Piedmont hazelnuts.

questions.q: In which year did Rowntree's of York launch the bar now known as KitKat?
questions.note: It appeared in 1935 as 'Rowntree's Chocolate Crisp', designed to fit in a working man's lunchbox.

questions.q: In which year did Otto Rohwedder's bread-slicing machine first sell sliced loaves commercially?
questions.note: A bakery in Chillicothe, Missouri sold the first machine-sliced loaves in 1928 — the benchmark for all great things since.

questions.q: In which year is pizza Margherita said to have been created in Naples for Queen Margherita of Savoy?
questions.note: In 1889 Raffaele Esposito topped a pizza with tomato, mozzarella and basil — red, white and green for the Italian flag.

questions.q: In which year did Vegemite first go on sale in Australia?
questions.note: Chemist Cyril Callister turned brewer's yeast into Vegemite in 1923, and Australians have argued about scraping thickness ever since.

questions.q: In which year did McDonald's introduce the Happy Meal?
questions.note: The Happy Meal arrived in 1979 with a circus-wagon box and a toy inside.

questions.q: In which year did Michelin publish its first restaurant and travel guide?
questions.note: The tyre company gave its first guide away free in 1900 to encourage the roughly 3,000 motorists then in France to drive more.

questions.q: In which year did Sobrino de Botín, the world's oldest restaurant, open in Madrid?
questions.note: Botín has been roasting suckling pig in the same wood-fired oven since 1725, says Guinness World Records.

questions.q: In which year did Nestlé launch Nescafé, the first mass-market instant coffee?
questions.note: Nescafé debuted in Switzerland in 1938 after seven years of work on turning surplus coffee into soluble powder.

questions.q: In which year did Daniel Peter of Vevey create the first milk chocolate?
questions.note: Peter cracked milk chocolate in 1875 using his neighbour Henri Nestlé's milk powder.

questions.q: In which year did J.S. Fry & Sons of Bristol mould the first solid eating-chocolate bar?
questions.note: Before Fry's 1847 bar, chocolate was almost always drunk rather than eaten.

questions.q: In which year did Roquefort become the first cheese protected by France's AOC system?
questions.source: Institut national de l'origine et de la qualité (INAO)
questions.note: Roquefort led the way in 1925, and it must still ripen in the natural caves of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon.

questions.q: In which year did the US Supreme Court rule that the tomato counts as a vegetable for tariff purposes?
questions.note: Botanically a fruit, legally a vegetable: the court settled it in 1893 because tomatoes are served with dinner, not dessert.

questions.q: In which year did New Zealand exporters rename the Chinese gooseberry the kiwifruit?
questions.source: Te Ara — The Encyclopedia of New Zealand
questions.note: The fuzzy brown fruit became the 'kiwifruit' in 1959, borrowing the name of the national bird.

questions.q: In which year did 12-year-old Edmond Albius invent the hand-pollination method still used for vanilla?
questions.note: In 1841 Albius, an enslaved boy on Réunion, found the quick thumb technique that made vanilla farming possible worldwide.

questions.q: In which year did Momofuku Ando invent instant ramen with Nissin's Chicken Ramen?
questions.note: Ando flash-fried noodles in his garden shed in 1958, creating one of the world's most eaten convenience foods.

questions.q: In which year did Caesar Cardini reportedly invent the Caesar salad in Tijuana, Mexico?
questions.note: The Caesar salad was born not in Rome but in Tijuana in 1924, tossed tableside during a busy holiday rush.

questions.q: In which year did Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya improvise the first plate of nachos in Piedras Negras?
questions.note: Anaya threw together fried tortillas, cheese and jalapeños for late customers in 1943 — and modestly named the dish after himself.

questions.q: In which year was the sandwich famously named after John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich?
questions.note: The story dates to 1762, when the Earl asked for beef between bread so he could eat without leaving the gaming table.

questions.q: In which year did Louis Pasteur patent his gentle heating process for preserving wine?
questions.note: Pasteur patented the process in 1865 to save French wine from spoiling — milk came later, but kept the name pasteurisation.

questions.q: In which year did Nicolas Appert win the French prize for preserving food in sealed containers?
questions.note: Appert collected 12,000 francs in 1810 for his glass-jar method — the birth of canning, decades before anyone knew why it worked.

questions.q: In which year was the Reinheitsgebot, the Bavarian beer purity law, issued?
questions.note: The 1516 decree allowed only water, barley and hops in beer — yeast had not yet been discovered.

questions.q: In which year did Sam Panopoulos first put pineapple on a pizza in Ontario, Canada?
questions.note: Hawaiian pizza is Canadian: Panopoulos tried tinned pineapple on a pizza in 1962, and the debate has never cooled.

questions.q: According to Chinese legend, in which year BC did Emperor Shennong discover tea when leaves blew into his boiling water?
questions.note: Legend dates tea to 2737 BC, when a stray leaf drifted into the emperor's freshly boiled water.

questions.q: At what temperature does water boil at sea level?
questions.note: Water boils at 100°C at sea level, but on Everest's summit it manages only about 70°C.

questions.q: To what internal temperature does the USDA say poultry should be cooked?
questions.note: The USDA's magic number is 74°C (165°F), the point at which poultry is reliably safe.

questions.q: At roughly what temperature does chocolate begin to melt?
questions.note: Cocoa butter melts at about 34°C — just below body temperature, which is why chocolate melts in the mouth.

questions.q: At about what temperature does table sugar begin to caramelise?
questions.note: Sucrose starts turning golden and complex at around 170°C, trading sweetness for hundreds of new flavour compounds.

questions.q: How hot must the dome of a wood-fired oven be for true Neapolitan pizza, per the AVPN?
questions.note: At the AVPN's required 485°C, a genuine Neapolitan pizza cooks in only 60 to 90 seconds.

questions.q: At what temperature is milk held for 15 seconds in standard HTST pasteurisation?
questions.note: Just 15 seconds at 72°C is enough to make milk safe while keeping its fresh taste.

questions.q: At how many bars of pressure is a proper Italian espresso extracted?
questions.note: Certified Italian espresso is pushed through the coffee at 9 bar — about three times the pressure in a car tyre.

questions.q: How many seconds should a certified Italian espresso take to extract?
questions.note: The institute specifies 25 seconds — quicker is sour and watery, slower turns bitter.

questions.q: What water temperature does the Specialty Coffee Association recommend for brewing filter coffee?
questions.note: The SCA's sweet spot is about 93°C — hot but off the boil, which scalds delicate aromatics.

questions.q: At about what oil temperature are chips and other foods typically deep-fried?
questions.note: Around 180°C the surface crisps and seals quickly, so the food fries instead of soaking up oil.

questions.q: At about what temperature does the Maillard browning reaction get going in earnest?
questions.note: From roughly 140°C, sugars and proteins begin the Maillard reaction that gives bread crusts and seared steaks their flavour.

questions.q: At about what internal temperature does a popcorn kernel finally pop?
questions.note: At about 180°C the steam inside wins, and the kernel turns itself inside out at close to 40 times its original volume.

questions.q: Gas mark 6 on a British oven corresponds to how many degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Gas mark 6 is 200°C — the workhorse setting for roast potatoes and countless British bakes.

questions.q: What is the recommended temperature for a home freezer?
questions.note: At -18°C (0°F) microbes stop growing, which is why it is the standard for home freezers worldwide.

questions.q: At about what temperature does sugar syrup reach the 'hard crack' stage used for lollipops and brittle?
questions.note: Around 150°C almost no water remains, so the cooled sugar snaps cleanly — the hard crack of lollipops and brittle.

questions.q: How many millilitres are in a standard metric tablespoon?
questions.note: A metric tablespoon is 15 ml — exactly three 5 ml teaspoons.

questions.q: How many teaspoons are in one US cup?
questions.note: A US cup holds 48 teaspoons, which is 16 tablespoons of 3 teaspoons each.

questions.q: How many litres are in a US gallon?
questions.note: A US gallon is about 3.8 litres — noticeably smaller than the 4.5-litre imperial gallon.

questions.q: How many items are in a baker's dozen?
questions.note: A baker's dozen is 13 — medieval bakers added a spare loaf to avoid harsh penalties for selling short weight.

questions.q: How many grams does a standard US stick of butter weigh?
questions.note: A US stick is a quarter pound — 113 g — and American recipes are built around it.

questions.q: How many millilitres are in a British imperial pint?
questions.note: The imperial pint is 568 ml, comfortably larger than the 473 ml US pint.

questions.q: How many grams does one US cup of all-purpose flour weigh?
questions.note: King Arthur's standard is 120 g per cup — spooned and levelled, never scooped and packed.

questions.q: How much does a US 'large' egg weigh in its shell, on average?
questions.note: US grading makes a large egg about 57 g in the shell — a dozen must total at least 680 g.

questions.q: How many millilitres does a standard wine bottle hold?
questions.source: International Organisation of Vine and Wine (OIV)
questions.note: The standard bottle is 750 ml, a size that became near-universal in the 1970s.

questions.q: What minimum percentage of cocoa butter must white chocolate contain under US FDA rules?
questions.note: White chocolate needs at least 20% cocoa butter — it contains cocoa fat but no dark cocoa solids at all.

questions.q: What minimum percentage of total dry cocoa solids must plain chocolate contain under EU law?
questions.note: EU rules set the bar at 35% cocoa solids for chocolate proper — fine bars often double that.

questions.q: Roughly how many cocoa beans does it take to make about 450 g of chocolate?
questions.note: It takes roughly 400 beans to make a pound of chocolate — each cacao pod supplies only a few dozen.

questions.q: How many milligrams of caffeine are in a typical 240 ml cup of brewed coffee?
questions.note: A standard cup carries about 95 mg of caffeine — roughly double what the same cup of black tea provides.

questions.q: How many main categories of true tea are traditionally made from the Camellia sinensis plant?
questions.note: All 6 — green, yellow, white, oolong, black and dark — come from one species, differing only in processing.

questions.q: About how many seeds does a typical cacao pod contain?
questions.note: A cacao pod holds about 40 seeds nestled in sweet white pulp — the raw material of all chocolate.

questions.q: What percentage of caffeine must be removed for coffee to be sold as decaffeinated in the US?
questions.note: US decaf must shed 97% of its caffeine, so a whisper of it always remains in the cup.

questions.q: How many varieties of cheese did Charles de Gaulle famously say made France impossible to govern?
questions.note: De Gaulle sighed over governing a country with 246 cheeses — modern counts put the real number far higher.

questions.q: For how many months, at minimum, must Parmigiano-Reggiano be aged?
questions.note: The legal minimum is 12 months — the longest ageing required of any European PDO cheese, and many wheels rest for three years.

questions.q: How much does a whole wheel of Parmigiano-Reggiano typically weigh?
questions.note: A wheel weighs about 40 kg and takes roughly 550 litres of milk to make.

questions.q: About how many named cheeses does Britain produce, according to the British Cheese Board?
questions.note: Britain quietly makes about 700 named cheeses — more, cheesemongers love to note, than France's famous count.

questions.q: About what percentage of the world's cheese ends up stolen, according to a 2011 retail study?
questions.note: Around 4% of cheese is stolen, making it the world's most shoplifted food.

questions.q: On average, how many seeds dot the outside of a single strawberry?
questions.note: A strawberry wears about 200 seeds on its skin — the only common fruit to carry them on the outside.

questions.q: What percentage of a watermelon is water?
questions.note: Watermelon is about 92% water, which is exactly what the name promised.

questions.q: What percentage of a cucumber is water?
questions.note: At about 95% water, the cucumber is one of the most water-rich foods on any plate.

questions.q: About what percentage of an apple's volume is air?
questions.note: Roughly 25% of an apple is air trapped between its cells — which is why apples bob so cheerfully.

questions.q: About what percentage of a banana is water?
questions.note: Even a dense, creamy banana is about 75% water.

questions.q: About how many varieties of apple are grown around the world?
questions.note: Some 7,500 apple varieties exist worldwide — trying one a day would take over 20 years.

questions.q: How many native potato varieties does the International Potato Center say grow in the Andes?
questions.note: The Andes hold over 4,000 native potato varieties in a riot of colours, shapes and sizes.

questions.q: About how many kernels are on an average ear of corn?
questions.note: An average ear packs about 800 kernels, almost always in an even 16 rows.

questions.q: How many Scoville heat units does pure capsaicin measure?
questions.note: Pure capsaicin clocks 16 million Scoville units — thousands of times hotter than a jalapeño.

questions.q: For up to how many years is Tabasco pepper mash aged in oak barrels?
questions.note: Tabasco mash rests in white-oak barrels for up to 3 years on Avery Island before becoming sauce.

questions.q: Roughly how many crocus flowers must be hand-picked to yield one pound (450 g) of saffron?
questions.note: About 75,000 blossoms give a single pound of saffron, each flower offering just three precious threads.

questions.q: For about how many months does Kikkoman brew its traditional soy sauce?
questions.note: Kikkoman's soy sauce ferments for about 6 months, developing some 300 flavour and aroma components.

questions.q: About how many flowers must honeybees visit to make 450 g of honey?
questions.note: It takes about 2 million flower visits to fill a single pound jar of honey.

questions.q: What is the maximum percentage of water honey may generally contain under the Codex Alimentarius standard?
questions.note: Honey must generally stay at or under 20% water — any wetter and it can ferment in the jar.

questions.q: What is the maximum free acidity, in percent, allowed for extra virgin olive oil?
questions.note: Extra virgin status demands free acidity of no more than 0.8% — plus passing a taste test for zero defects.

questions.q: What minimum percentage of milkfat must US ice cream contain to be labelled ice cream?
questions.note: US ice cream must be at least 10% milkfat — premium tubs often carry 16% or more.

questions.q: What minimum percentage of milkfat must butter contain in the United States?
questions.note: Butter must be at least 80% milkfat, a standard shared by the EU.

questions.q: About how many peanuts does it take to make a 340 g jar of peanut butter?
questions.note: Roughly 540 peanuts are ground into every 12-ounce jar of peanut butter.

questions.q: About how many kilograms of olives does it take to produce one litre of olive oil?
questions.note: Around 5 kg of olives are pressed for each litre of oil — a whole small tree's harvest in a couple of bottles.

questions.q: About how many litres of water does it take to grow one kilogram of rice?
questions.note: Growing a kilo of rice drinks about 2,500 litres of water, mostly in flooded paddies.

questions.q: How many varieties of kimchi are documented by Seoul's Museum Kimchikan?
questions.note: The museum documents 187 kimchi varieties, from classic cabbage to cucumber, radish and beyond.

questions.q: About how many kilograms of pasta does the average Italian eat per year?
questions.note: Italians lead the world at about 23 kg of pasta per person per year, well ahead of second-placed Tunisia at around 17 kg.

questions.q: How much does a traditional French baguette weigh?
questions.source: Confédération Nationale de la Boulangerie Française
questions.note: The classic baguette weighs about 250 g and is best eaten within hours of baking.

questions.q: How many square metres was the largest pizza ever made, baked in Rome in 2012?
questions.note: The record 'Ottavia' pizza covered 1,261 m² — and was entirely gluten-free.

questions.q: Madagascar has long produced about what percentage of the world's natural vanilla?
questions.note: Around 80% of natural vanilla comes from Madagascar, mostly hand-pollinated on small family farms.

questions.q: Roughly how many billion fortune cookies are made worldwide each year?
questions.note: About 3 billion fortune cookies are baked yearly — nearly all in the United States, not China.

questions.q: How many years long is the lease Arthur Guinness signed in 1759 for his Dublin brewery?
questions.note: Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease on St James's Gate at £45 a year — quite the show of confidence.

questions.q: How many bars of pressure are inside a bottle of champagne?
questions.note: A champagne cork holds back about 6 bars of pressure — roughly triple a car tyre.

questions.q: How many years old is the world's oldest known winery, found in Armenia's Areni-1 cave?
questions.note: The Areni-1 cave winery is about 6,100 years old, complete with a grape press and fermentation jars.

questions.q: How many 'official flavours' does Jelly Belly maintain?
questions.note: Jelly Belly keeps 50 official flavours, from Very Cherry to the polarising Buttered Popcorn.

questions.q: What number of 'varieties' has Heinz famously advertised since the 1890s?
questions.note: Henry Heinz picked '57 Varieties' because he liked the number — the company already sold more than 60 products.

questions.q: How many herbs and spices are in KFC's famous secret recipe?
questions.note: Colonel Sanders' recipe counts 11 herbs and spices, reputedly kept in a vault in Louisville.

questions.q: How many US cents did a glass of Coca-Cola cost when it launched in 1886?
questions.note: A glass cost 5 cents in 1886 — and, remarkably, the nickel price held for over 70 years.

questions.q: How many standard colours are in a bag of milk chocolate M&M's?
questions.note: There are 6 standard colours — blue joined red, orange, yellow, green and brown after a public vote in 1995.

questions.q: In which year was Toblerone created in Bern, Switzerland?
questions.note: 1908 — its triangular peaks were trademarked, and Bern's bear still hides in the mountain logo.

questions.q: How many bones are in the adult human skeleton?
questions.note: An adult has 206 bones, over half of them tucked into the hands and feet.

questions.q: Roughly how many bones does a newborn baby have?
questions.note: Babies start with about 300 bones, many of which fuse together to leave the adult 206.

questions.q: How many bones are in one human hand, including the wrist?
questions.source: American Society for Surgery of the Hand
questions.note: Each hand packs in 27 bones, which is why it can manage everything from piano to origami.

questions.q: How many bones are in one human foot, including the ankle?
questions.note: Each foot has 26 bones, working with 33 joints to cushion every step you take.

questions.q: How many bones make up the adult human skull?
questions.note: The skull is a jigsaw of 22 bones, 8 cradling the brain and 14 shaping the face.

questions.q: How many vertebrae, counting the fused segments of the sacrum and tailbone, make up the human spine?
questions.note: The spine is built from 33 vertebrae, the lowest nine of which fuse together as we grow.

questions.q: How many ribs does a typical human have?
questions.note: We have 24 ribs in 12 pairs, forming a flexible cage that moves with every breath.

questions.q: How long, in millimetres, is the stapes, the smallest bone in the human body?
questions.note: The stirrup-shaped stapes in your middle ear is just 3 mm long, smaller than a grain of rice.

questions.q: How many vertebrae are in the human neck?
questions.note: The neck has 7 vertebrae, exactly the same number as a giraffe's, just far shorter.

questions.q: How many tiny bones are inside each human middle ear?
questions.note: Each middle ear holds 3 miniature bones, the hammer, anvil and stirrup, that relay sound to the inner ear.

questions.q: How many bones in the human body are not connected to any other bone?
questions.note: Just 1, the hyoid bone in the throat, floats free, anchored only by muscles, and helps us speak and swallow.

questions.q: What percentage of an adult's body weight is the skeleton?
questions.note: The whole skeleton is only about 15% of your body weight, a marvel of lightweight engineering.

questions.q: Roughly how many years does it take the adult skeleton to completely renew itself?
questions.note: Bone is living tissue that replaces itself about every 10 years, so your skeleton is far younger than you are.

questions.q: What percentage of the body's calcium is stored in the bones and teeth?
questions.note: A remarkable 99% of your calcium lives in your bones and teeth, which double as the body's mineral bank.

questions.q: How many teeth are in a complete adult set, including wisdom teeth?
questions.note: A full adult set has 32 teeth, each one coated in enamel that must last a lifetime.

questions.q: How many baby teeth does a child grow?
questions.note: Children grow 20 baby teeth, placeholders that guide the adult set into position.

questions.q: What is tooth enamel's hardness on the 1-to-10 Mohs mineral scale?
questions.note: Enamel scores 5 on the Mohs scale, making it the hardest substance the human body produces.

questions.q: Roughly how many skeletal muscles are in the human body?
questions.note: You have roughly 600 skeletal muscles, and anatomists still quibble over the exact count.

questions.q: How many muscles move each human eye?
questions.note: Each eye is steered by 6 muscles, among the fastest and most precise in the whole body.

questions.q: How many muscles make up the human tongue?
questions.note: The tongue is a team of 8 muscles working together for speech, taste and swallowing.

questions.q: About how many litres of blood does an average adult have?
questions.note: An adult carries about 5 litres of blood, and the heart cycles all of it round the body every minute.

questions.q: About how many times does the human heart beat in one day?
questions.note: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day without ever taking a rest.

questions.q: About how many billion times does the average human heart beat in a lifetime?
questions.note: Over a lifetime the heart beats about 2.5 billion times, a rhythm that starts before birth.

questions.q: About how many litres of blood does the heart pump in a single day?
questions.note: The heart moves about 7,500 litres a day, enough to fill a small road tanker.

questions.q: About how many litres of blood does the resting heart pump each minute?
questions.note: At rest the heart pumps about 5 litres a minute, your entire blood supply in one lap.

questions.q: About how much does an adult human heart weigh, in grams?
questions.note: The heart weighs about 300 grams, roughly the same as a large orange, yet powers your whole life.

questions.q: Laid end to end, about how many kilometres of blood vessels are in one human body?
questions.note: Your blood vessels stretch about 100,000 km, enough to circle the Earth more than twice.

questions.q: About how many days does a red blood cell live?
questions.note: A red blood cell lives about 120 days, making roughly 250,000 laps of the body before retiring.

questions.q: About how many million new red blood cells does your body make every second?
questions.note: Your bone marrow releases about 2 million fresh red blood cells every single second.

questions.q: What percentage of blood is plasma, the straw-coloured liquid part?
questions.note: Blood is about 55% plasma, a golden fluid that ferries nutrients, hormones and warmth around the body.

questions.q: How many main blood groups are there in the ABO system?
questions.note: The ABO system has 4 main groups, A, B, AB and O, discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1901.

questions.q: About how wide, in centimetres, is the aorta, the body's largest artery?
questions.note: The aorta is about 2.5 cm across, roughly the width of a garden hose.

questions.q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
questions.note: The heart has 4 chambers, two atria and two ventricles, beating in perfect coordination.

questions.q: About how many litres of air can adult lungs hold at their fullest?
questions.note: Fully inflated, adult lungs hold about 6 litres of air, roughly three large fizzy-drink bottles.

questions.q: About how many breaths does a person take in a day?
questions.note: You take about 20,000 breaths a day, almost all of them without a single thought.

questions.q: About how many million alveoli, the tiny air sacs, are in a pair of human lungs?
questions.source: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
questions.note: Careful counts put the average at about 480 million alveoli, each one swapping oxygen with the blood.

questions.q: Spread flat, about how many square metres of surface area do the lungs have inside?
questions.note: Unfolded, the lungs' gas-exchange surface covers about 70 square metres — roughly a third of a tennis court, packed into your chest.

questions.q: About how many millilitres of air does one relaxed breath move in and out?
questions.note: A quiet breath shifts about 500 ml of air, roughly a large glass of water's worth.

questions.q: How many lobes does the right human lung have?
questions.note: The right lung has 3 lobes while the left makes do with 2, leaving room for the heart.

questions.q: About how much does an adult human brain weigh, in kilograms?
questions.note: The brain weighs about 1.4 kg, yet holds every memory, skill and dream you have.

questions.q: About how many billion neurons are in the human brain?
questions.note: Careful counting revealed about 86 billion neurons, dethroning the old estimate of 100 billion.

questions.q: What percentage of the body's energy does the brain use?
questions.note: The brain burns about 20% of your energy despite being only about 2% of your weight.

questions.q: What percentage of the human brain is water?
questions.note: The brain is about 73% water, which is why even mild dehydration can fog your thinking.

questions.q: How fast, in metres per second, can the quickest human nerve signals travel?
questions.note: The fastest nerve fibres fire signals at about 120 metres per second, over 400 km/h.

questions.q: About how many trillion synapses, or neural connections, does an adult brain contain?
questions.note: The adult brain holds roughly 100 trillion synapses, more connections than there are stars in a thousand Milky Ways... almost.

questions.q: About how long, in centimetres, is the adult human spinal cord?
questions.note: The spinal cord is about 45 cm long, a data cable thinner than your finger carrying everything the body says to the brain.

questions.q: By age five, what percentage of its adult size has the human brain reached?
questions.note: By age five the brain has already reached about 90% of its adult size, growth no other organ can match.

questions.q: In a baby's brain, about how many million new neural connections can form every second?
questions.note: In the first years of life, more than 1 million new neural connections form every second.

questions.q: By one famous estimate, how many petabytes of information could the human brain store?
questions.note: One estimate puts the brain's capacity at 2.5 petabytes, enough for around three million hours of TV.

questions.q: Up to how long, in metres, can a single human nerve cell be?
questions.note: Neurons serving the sciatic nerve can stretch about 1 metre, from the base of the spine to the toes.

questions.q: What is the upper limit of human hearing, in hertz, for a healthy young ear?
questions.note: Young ears hear up to about 20,000 Hz, a ceiling that dogs and bats sail far beyond.

questions.q: About how many million different colours can the human eye distinguish?
questions.note: The human eye can tell apart an estimated 10 million colours, far more than any screen can show.

questions.q: About how wide, in millimetres, is an adult human eyeball?
questions.note: The eyeball is about 24 mm across, almost fully grown by the time you finish primary school.

questions.q: About how many million rod cells for night vision does each human eye contain?
questions.note: Each eye has about 120 million rod cells, sensitive enough to respond to a single photon of light.

questions.q: About how many different types of smell receptor does the human nose have?
questions.note: With about 400 receptor types working in combination, the nose can pick apart an astonishing range of scents.

questions.q: About how many taste buds does the average person have?
questions.note: The average person has about 10,000 taste buds, and they are not just on the tongue but the roof of the mouth too.

questions.q: About every how many days are your taste buds replaced with new ones?
questions.note: Taste buds renew about every 10 days, so your sense of taste is constantly rebuilt from scratch.

questions.q: How small a surface bump, in nanometres, can a human fingertip detect?
questions.note: Fingertips can feel ridges just 13 nanometres tall; scaled up to Earth size, that is like feeling a car under your finger.

questions.q: How close, in centimetres, can a young adult eye comfortably focus on fine print?
questions.note: The classic near point of the eye is about 25 cm, the standard reading distance in optics.

questions.q: How many different types of tears do human eyes produce?
questions.note: Eyes make 3 kinds of tears, basal, reflex and emotional, and each has a different chemical recipe.

questions.q: About how many square metres of skin cover an average adult?
questions.note: Your skin, the body's largest organ, covers about 2 square metres, roughly the top of a double bed.

questions.q: About every how many days does the outer layer of your skin completely replace itself?
questions.note: The epidermis renews itself about every 28 days, meaning you wear a brand-new surface every month.

questions.q: About how many centimetres does human head hair grow in a year?
questions.note: Head hair grows about 15 cm a year, making hair follicles some of the busiest tissue in the body.

questions.q: About how many hairs are on a typical human head?
questions.note: A typical scalp holds about 100,000 hairs, each growing from its own tiny follicle.

questions.q: Up to how many hairs does a person naturally shed each day?
questions.note: Shedding up to 100 hairs a day is perfectly normal, and the follicles simply grow replacements.

questions.q: About how many millimetres do fingernails grow in a month?
questions.note: Fingernails grow about 3.5 mm a month, and the nails on your longer fingers grow slightly faster.

questions.q: How thick, in millimetres, is the skin of the eyelid, the thinnest on the body?
questions.note: Eyelid skin is only about 0.5 mm thick, delicate enough to let a hint of morning light through.

questions.q: About how many million hair follicles are on the entire human body?
questions.note: You have about 5 million hair follicles all over your body, about the same number as a chimpanzee.

questions.q: About how many trillion cells make up an adult human body?
questions.note: A landmark tally arrived at about 37.2 trillion cells, every one descended from a single fertilised egg.

questions.q: Stretched out, about how many metres of DNA are coiled inside a single human cell?
questions.note: Each cell packs about 2 metres of DNA into a nucleus far thinner than a human hair.

questions.q: About how many billion base pairs, or DNA letters, are in the human genome?
questions.note: The human genome runs to about 3 billion base pairs, a text that would fill a bookcase of encyclopaedias.

questions.q: About how many protein-coding genes does the human genome contain?
questions.note: Humans have only about 20,000 protein-coding genes, similar to a microscopic roundworm, yet look what they build.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are in a typical human cell?
questions.note: Human cells carry 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, one of each pair from each parent.

questions.q: What percentage of their DNA do any two humans share?
questions.note: Any two people are 99.9% genetically identical; all human variety lives in the remaining 0.1%.

questions.q: In which year was the Human Genome Project declared complete?
questions.note: The Human Genome Project was completed in 2003, fifty years almost to the month after the double helix was found.

questions.q: About how many distinct types of cell make up the human body?
questions.note: The body is built from about 200 cell types, from metre-long neurons to disc-shaped red blood cells.

questions.q: About how many billion cells does your body replace every day?
questions.note: Your body swaps out about 330 billion cells a day, most of them blood and gut cells, without you noticing a thing.

questions.q: How wide, in millimetres, is the human egg cell, the largest cell in the body?
questions.note: At about 0.1 mm, the egg cell is the only human cell big enough to see with the naked eye.

questions.q: About how many minutes does one full human sleep cycle last?
questions.note: A sleep cycle lasts about 90 minutes, and we glide through four to six of them every night.

questions.q: How many distinct stages make up one human sleep cycle?
questions.note: Each cycle moves through 4 stages, three of quiet non-REM sleep and one of vivid REM.

questions.q: What percentage of a typical human life is spent asleep?
questions.note: We sleep for about 33% of our lives, roughly 26 years of essential, restorative rest.

questions.q: About how many hours a day does a newborn baby sleep?
questions.note: Newborns sleep about 16 hours a day, busily wiring their brains while they doze.

questions.q: About how many hours a night does the average person spend dreaming?
questions.note: We spend about 2 hours a night dreaming, whether or not we remember a moment of it.

questions.q: How many hours long is the human internal body clock's natural cycle?
questions.note: Our built-in clock runs on a cycle of about 24.2 hours, gently reset each morning by daylight.

questions.q: What is the classic average human body temperature, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: The textbook figure is 37 °C, held steady by the brain's hypothalamus acting as a thermostat.

questions.q: About what percentage of an adult human body is water?
questions.note: An adult body is about 60% water, sloshing through cells, blood and even bones.

questions.q: About what percentage of the human body's mass is the element oxygen?
questions.note: Oxygen makes up about 65% of your mass, mostly locked into the water in your cells.

questions.q: About how many grams of iron does an adult human body contain?
questions.note: Your body holds about 4 grams of iron, enough for a small nail, most of it busy carrying oxygen in your blood.

questions.q: About how many litres of fluid do your kidneys filter from the blood each day?
questions.note: The kidneys filter about 180 litres a day, reclaiming almost all of it in a marvel of recycling.

questions.q: About how many million filtering units, or nephrons, are in each human kidney?
questions.note: Each kidney contains about 1 million nephrons, microscopic filters working around the clock.

questions.q: About how many metres long is the human small intestine?
questions.note: The small intestine is about 6 metres long, neatly folded to fit inside your abdomen.

questions.q: About how much does the adult human liver weigh, in kilograms?
questions.note: The liver weighs about 1.5 kg, the heaviest organ inside the body and a tireless chemical factory.

questions.q: What is the approximate pH of human stomach acid?
questions.note: Stomach acid sits around pH 2, and a fresh mucus lining keeps it from digesting the stomach itself.

questions.q: About how many watts of heat does a resting human body give off?
questions.note: At rest you radiate about 100 watts, quietly warming the room like an old-fashioned light bulb.

questions.q: Up to how many centimetres taller can astronauts grow while living in space?
questions.note: Freed from gravity, astronauts' spines stretch up to 5 cm, though the extra height fades back on Earth.

questions.q: How tall, in centimetres, was Robert Wadlow, the tallest person ever reliably measured?
questions.note: Robert Wadlow reached 272 cm, and his gentle manner earned him the nickname the Alton Giant.

questions.q: To what age, in years, did Jeanne Calment, the longest-lived person on record, live?
questions.note: Jeanne Calment lived to 122, took up fencing at 85 and rode a bicycle at 100.

questions.q: How many weeks does a typical full-term human pregnancy last?
questions.note: A full-term pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks, during which a single cell becomes trillions.

questions.q: At birth, about what percentage of a baby's total body length is its head?
questions.note: A newborn's head is about 25% of its body length, making room for that fast-growing brain.

questions.q: What percentage of a newborn baby's body is water?
questions.note: About 78% at birth, dropping to roughly 60% in adulthood.

questions.q: What is the atomic number of iron?
questions.note: Iron is element 26, and its symbol Fe comes from ferrum, the Latin word for the metal.

questions.q: What is the atomic number of oxygen?
questions.note: Oxygen is element 8, the gas that makes up about a fifth of the air you breathe.

questions.q: How many noble gases occur naturally on Earth?
questions.note: Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon occur naturally. Oganesson, the seventh, is made in the lab.

questions.q: At what temperature does copper melt, in degrees Celsius?
questions.note: Copper melts at 1,085 degrees Celsius, a little hotter than gold and well below iron.

questions.q: How fast does the Earth travel around the Sun, in kilometres per hour?
questions.note: Earth races around the Sun at about 107,000 kilometres per hour, and you are along for the ride.

questions.q: How many Earth days does Mercury take to orbit the Sun?
questions.note: A year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days, the shortest year of any planet.

questions.q: How many Earth days does Venus take to orbit the Sun?
questions.note: Venus circles the Sun in 225 Earth days, which is shorter than the time it takes to spin once.

questions.q: About how many years pass between returns of Halley's Comet?
questions.note: Halley's Comet swings by about every 76 years. Its last visit was in 1986, and the next is due in 2061.

questions.q: What is the temperature at the centre of the Sun, in millions of degrees Celsius?
questions.note: The Sun's core burns at about 15 million degrees Celsius, hot enough to fuse hydrogen into helium.

questions.q: In which year did NASA's Curiosity rover land in Gale Crater on Mars?
questions.note: Curiosity touched down in Gale Crater on 6 August 2012 and has been roaming Mars ever since.

questions.q: How many legs does an adult insect have?
questions.note: Six legs is the insect rule. Spiders, with eight, belong to a different branch of the animal kingdom.

questions.q: How many legs does a spider have?
questions.note: Spiders walk on 8 legs. Those extra 'feelers' near the mouth are pedipalps, not legs.

questions.q: How many teeth does an adult cat have in a full set?
questions.note: An adult cat has 30 teeth. Kittens start with 26 baby teeth, which they lose by about six months.

questions.q: How many arms does an octopus have?
questions.note: An octopus has 8 arms, each lined with suckers it can control on its own.

questions.q: How many teeth does an adult dog have in a full set?
questions.note: An adult dog has 42 teeth, ten more than a full adult human set.

questions.q: How long is the Mississippi River from Lake Itasca to the Gulf of Mexico, in kilometres?
questions.note: The USGS measures the Mississippi at 2,340 miles, which is 3,766 kilometres, from Lake Itasca to the Gulf.

questions.q: How high is the Canadian Horseshoe Falls at Niagara, in metres?
questions.note: The Horseshoe Falls drop 57 metres. Angel Falls is far taller, but nothing matches Niagara for the sheer volume of water.

questions.q: How tall is Mount Elbrus, the highest peak in Europe, in metres?
questions.note: Elbrus, a dormant volcano in the Caucasus, tops out at 5,642 metres, the highest point in Europe.

questions.q: How many Great Lakes are there in North America?
questions.note: Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario — five Great Lakes, holding about a fifth of the world's surface fresh water.

questions.q: How wide is the Strait of Dover at its narrowest point, in kilometres?
questions.note: At its narrowest the Strait of Dover is about 33 kilometres, close enough that on a clear day you can see across.

questions.q: In which year did Christopher Columbus first reach the Americas?
questions.note: Columbus sighted land in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492, after 70 days at sea.

questions.q: In which year was the United States Declaration of Independence adopted?
questions.note: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776.

questions.q: In which year was the Bastille stormed, the flashpoint of the French Revolution?
questions.note: A Paris crowd stormed the Bastille on 14 July 1789. Only seven prisoners were inside.

questions.q: In which year did the First World War begin in Europe?
questions.note: War broke out in the summer of 1914 after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo.

questions.q: In which year did the Berlin Wall open, after 28 years dividing the city?
questions.note: On the night of 9 November 1989, crowds poured through the Berlin Wall and began pulling it down.

questions.q: In which year was Steven Spielberg's Jaws released?
questions.note: Jaws opened in 1975 and became the first film to gross 100 million dollars in North America.

questions.q: In which year was Back to the Future released?
questions.note: Back to the Future hit cinemas in 1985, sending Marty McFly to the very year it was made... plus or minus thirty.

questions.q: In which year was Disney's The Lion King first released in cinemas?
questions.note: The Lion King opened in 1994 and became the highest-grossing traditionally animated film ever made.

questions.q: In which year was James Cameron's Titanic released?
questions.note: Titanic reached cinemas in 1997 and went on to tie the record with 11 Academy Awards.

questions.q: In which year was The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring released?
questions.note: The Fellowship of the Ring opened in December 2001, the first chapter of Peter Jackson's Middle-earth trilogy.

questions.q: To the nearest whole number, at how many revolutions per minute does a 12-inch vinyl LP spin?
questions.note: A long-playing record spins at 33⅓ rpm. Singles, by contrast, spin at 45.

questions.q: In which year was Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart born?
questions.note: Mozart was born in Salzburg on 27 January 1756 and wrote his first symphony at the age of eight.

questions.q: How many members were in Queen's classic line-up?
questions.note: Freddie Mercury, Brian May, Roger Taylor and John Deacon — Queen's classic four.

questions.q: How many white keys does a full-size piano have?
questions.note: Of a piano's 88 keys, 52 are white and 36 are black.

questions.q: How many Gymnopédies did Erik Satie compose?
questions.note: Satie wrote three Gymnopédies in the late 1880s, spare piano pieces that still turn up everywhere.

questions.q: How many innings are in a regulation game of baseball?
questions.note: A regulation baseball game lasts 9 innings, and only a tie or a rainout sends it further.

questions.q: How many feet separate consecutive bases on a baseball diamond?
questions.note: The bases sit 90 feet apart, a distance unchanged since the rules were standardised in the 19th century.

questions.q: How many players does an ice hockey team have on the ice, including the goalkeeper?
questions.note: Ice hockey puts 6 players on the ice: a goalkeeper, two defenders and three forwards.

questions.q: How many pins are set up in a standard game of ten-pin bowling?
questions.note: Ten pins stand in a triangle. Knock them all down on the first ball and that is a strike.

questions.q: In which year was the first Super Bowl played?
questions.note: Super Bowl I was played on 15 January 1967, and the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs.

questions.q: How many kilocalories does one gram of fat provide?
questions.note: Fat provides 9 kilocalories per gram. Carbohydrate and protein provide 4 each.

questions.q: How many kilocalories does one gram of carbohydrate provide?
questions.note: Carbohydrate provides 4 kilocalories per gram, the same as protein and less than half of fat.

questions.q: What minimum percentage of milkfat must US whole milk contain?
questions.note: Under US rules, whole milk must contain at least 3.25 percent milkfat.

questions.q: How many millilitres of coffee, including the crema, are in a certified Italian espresso?
questions.note: A certified Italian espresso is 25 millilitres in the cup, crema included, pulled in about 25 seconds.

questions.q: About how many litres of maple sap does it take to make one litre of maple syrup?
questions.source: Producteurs et productrices acéricoles du Québec
questions.note: It takes about 40 litres of sap to boil down into a single litre of maple syrup.

questions.q: How many lobes does the left human lung have?
questions.note: The left lung has 2 lobes, leaving room for the heart. The right lung has 3.

questions.q: What is the normal pH of human blood?
questions.note: Healthy blood sits at about pH 7.4, just on the alkaline side of neutral.

questions.q: According to the American Heart Association, a normal adult resting heart rate runs up to how many beats per minute?
questions.note: A normal resting heart rate for adults is 60 to 100 beats per minute. Athletes often sit lower.

questions.q: How many phalanges, the finger bones, are in one human hand?
questions.note: Each hand has 14 phalanges: three in each finger and two in the thumb.

questions.q: How many pairs of cranial nerves branch from the human brain?
questions.note: Twelve pairs of cranial nerves leave the brain, handling everything from smell and sight to the muscles of the face.
